'''Mars''' is the fourth [[planet]] from the [[Sun]]. It is also known as the "'''Red Planet'''",<ref name="nasa-facts">{{Cite web |title=Mars: Facts |website=NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/mars/facts/ |access-date=7 September 2026 |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260704063354/https://science.nasa.gov/mars/facts/ |archive-date=4 July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> for [[Mars surface color|its orange-red]] appearance.<ref name="Rees2012">{{cite book |title=Universe: The Definitive Visual Guide |date=October 2012 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |isbn=978-0-7566-9841-6 |editor-last=Rees |editor-first=Martin J. |location=New York |pages=160–161}}</ref><ref name="nasa_hematite" /> Mars is a desert-like [[rocky planet]] with a tenuous [[Atmosphere of Mars|atmosphere]] that is primarily [[carbon dioxide]] ({{chem2|CO2}}). At the average surface level the atmospheric pressure is a few thousandths of [[Earth]]'s, atmospheric temperature ranges from {{Cvt|-153|to|20|C|F}},<ref name="nasa-facts"/> and [[cosmic radiation]] is high. Mars retains some water, [[Groundwater on Mars|in the ground]] as well as thinly in the atmosphere, forming [[cirrus cloud]]s, [[fog]], [[frost]], larger polar regions of [[permafrost]] and [[Martian polar ice caps|ice caps]] (with seasonal {{chem2|CO2}} snow), but no bodies of liquid surface water. Its surface gravity is roughly a third of Earth's or double that of the Moon. Its mean diameter, {{Cvt|6779|km|4=0}},<ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Matthew |date=21 June 2016 |title=What Are The Diameters of the Planets? |url=https://www.universetoday.com/articles/diameters-of-the-planets |access-date=11 June 2026 |website=Universe Today |language=en}}</ref> is about [[List of Solar System objects by size|half the Earth]]'s, or twice the Moon's, and its surface area is around the size of all the dry land of Earth.<ref name="nasa-facts"/>

[[Martian regolith#Atmospheric dust|Fine dust]] is prevalent across the surface and the atmosphere, being picked up and spread at the low Martian gravity even by the weak wind of the tenuous atmosphere.
The terrain of Mars roughly follows a north–south divide, the [[Martian dichotomy]], with the northern hemisphere mainly consisting of relatively flat, low lying [[plain]]s, and the southern hemisphere of cratered [[highland]]s. [[Geology of Mars|Geologically]], the planet is fairly active with [[marsquake]]s trembling underneath the ground, but also hosts many enormous [[volcano]]es that are extinct (the tallest is [[Olympus Mons]], {{Convert|21.9|km|mi|abbr=on|disp=or}} tall), as well as one of the largest [[canyon]]s in the Solar System ([[Valles Marineris]], {{Convert|4000|km|mi|abbr=on|disp=or}} long). Mars has [[Moons of Mars|two natural satellites]] that are small and irregular in shape: [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]] and [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]]. With a significant [[axial tilt]] of 25&nbsp;degrees, Mars experiences [[season]]s, like Earth (which has an axial tilt of 23.5&nbsp;degrees). A [[Timekeeping on Mars|Martian solar year]] is equal to 1.88&nbsp;Earth years (687&nbsp;Earth days), a Martian solar day ([[Mars sol|sol]]) is equal to 24.6&nbsp;hours.

Mars formed along with the other planets approximately 4.5&nbsp;billion years ago. During the martian [[Noachian]] period (4.5 to 3.5&nbsp;billion years ago), its surface was marked by [[Impact event|meteor impacts]], valley formation, erosion, the [[Mars ocean theory|possible presence of water ocean]]s and the loss of its [[magnetosphere]]. The [[Hesperian]] period (beginning 3.5&nbsp;billion years ago and ending 3.3–2.9&nbsp;billion years ago) was dominated by widespread [[Volcanism|volcanic activity]] and flooding that carved immense [[outflow channels]]. The [[Amazonian (Mars)|Amazonian]] period, which continues to the present, is the currently dominating and remaining [[Aeolian processes|influence on geological processes]]. Because of Mars's geological history, the possibility of past or present [[life on Mars]] remains an area of active scientific investigation, with some possible traces needing further examination.

Being [[Apparent magnitude|visible]] with the naked eye in Earth's sky as a red [[classical planet|wandering star]], Mars has been [[History of Mars observation|observed throughout history]], acquiring diverse associations in different cultures. In 1963 the first flight to Mars took place with [[Mars 1]], but communication was lost en route. The first successful flyby [[exploration of Mars]] was conducted in 1965 with [[Mariner 4]]. In 1971 [[Mariner 9]] entered orbit around Mars, being the first spacecraft to orbit any body other than the Moon, Sun or Earth; following in the same year were the first uncontrolled impact ([[Mars 2]]) and first successful landing ([[Mars 3]]) on Mars. Probes have been active on Mars continuously since 1997. At times, more than ten [[List of missions to Mars|probes have simultaneously operated]] in orbit or on the surface, more than at any other planet beyond Earth.<!-- Orbiters and rovers are too numerous to all be named here. The active probe list is more suitable at the Exploration section. --> Mars is an often proposed target for future [[Human mission to Mars|crewed exploration missions]], though no such mission is currently planned.

== Natural history ==
{{Main|Geological history of Mars}}

=== Formation ===
Scientists have theorized that during the [[Formation and evolution of the Solar System|Solar System's formation]], Mars was created as the result of a [[stochastic process|random process]] of run-away [[Accretion (astrophysics)|accretion]] of material from the [[protoplanetary disk]] that orbited the Sun. Mars has many distinctive chemical features caused by its position in the Solar System. Elements with comparatively low boiling points, such as [[chlorine]], [[phosphorus]], and [[sulfur]], are much more common on Mars than on Earth; these elements were probably pushed outward by the young Sun's energetic [[solar wind]].<ref name="ssr96_1_4_197"/>

=== Late Heavy Bombardment ===
After the formation of the planets, the inner Solar System may have been subjected to the so-called [[Late Heavy Bombardment]]. About 60% of the surface of Mars shows a record of impacts from that era,<ref name="zharkov93" /><ref name="icarus165_1" /><ref name="barlow88" /> whereas much of the remaining surface is probably underlain by immense impact basins caused by those events. However, more recent modeling has disputed the existence of the Late Heavy Bombardment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nesvorný |first1=David |date=June 2018 |title=Dynamical Evolution of the Early Solar System |journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=56 |pages=137–174 |doi=10.1146/annurev-astro-081817-052028 |arxiv=1807.06647 |bibcode=2018ARA&A..56..137N}}</ref> There is evidence of an enormous impact basin in the Northern Hemisphere of Mars, spanning {{convert|10600|by|8500|km}}, or roughly four times the size of the Moon's [[South Pole–Aitken basin]], which would be the largest impact basin yet discovered if confirmed.<ref name="northcratersn" /> It has been hypothesized that the basin was formed when Mars was struck by a [[Pluto]]-sized body about four billion years ago. The event, thought to be the cause of the [[Martian dichotomy|Martian hemispheric dichotomy]], created the smooth [[Borealis basin]] that covers 40% of the planet.<ref name="sciam080627" /><ref name="nyt080626" />

A 2023 study shows evidence, based on the [[orbital inclination]] of [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]] (a small [[natural satellite|moon]] of Mars), that Mars may once have had a [[ring system]] 3.5&nbsp;billion years to 4&nbsp;billion years ago.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ćuk |first1=Matija |last2=Minton |first2=David A. |last3=Pouplin |first3=Jennifer L. L. |last4=Wishard |first4=Carlisle |date=16 June 2020 |title=Evidence for a Past Martian Ring from the Orbital Inclination of Deimos |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=896 |issue=2 |pages=L28 |doi=10.3847/2041-8213/ab974f |arxiv=2006.00645 |bibcode=2020ApJ...896L..28C |issn=2041-8213 |doi-access=free}}</ref> This ring system may have been formed from a moon, 20 times more [[mass]]ive than [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]], orbiting Mars billions of years ago; and Phobos would be a remnant of that ring.<ref>{{Cite web |author=News Staff |date=4 June 2020 |title=Researchers Find New Evidence that Mars Once Had Massive Ring {{!}} Sci.News |url=https://www.sci.news/space/ancient-mars-ring-08502.html |access-date=7 November 2023 |website=Sci.News: Breaking Science News |archive-date=7 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231107064634/https://www.sci.news/space/ancient-mars-ring-08502.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=5 June 2020 |title=Did ancient Mars have rings? |url=https://earthsky.org/space/did-ancient-mars-have-rings-deimos/ |access-date=7 November 2023 |newspaper=Earthsky &#124; Updates on Your Cosmos and World |archive-date=7 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231107064635/https://earthsky.org/space/did-ancient-mars-have-rings-deimos/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Geological periods ===
{{Mars timescale}}

The geological history of Mars can be split into many periods, but the following are the three primary periods:<ref name="jog91" /><ref name="ssr_96_1_4" />
* [[Noachian]] period: Formation of the oldest extant surfaces of Mars, 4.5 to 3.5&nbsp;billion years ago. Noachian age surfaces are scarred by many large impact craters. The [[Tharsis]] bulge, a volcanic upland, is thought to have formed during this period, with extensive flooding by liquid water late in the period. Named after [[Noachis Terra]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=ESA Science & Technology – The Ages of Mars |url=https://sci.esa.int/web/mars-express/-/55481-the-ages-of-mars |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829030639/https://sci.esa.int/web/mars-express/-/55481-the-ages-of-mars |archive-date=29 August 2023 |access-date=7 December 2021 |website=sci.esa.int}}</ref>
* [[Hesperian]] period: 3.5 to between 3.3 and 2.9&nbsp;billion years ago. The Hesperian period is marked by the formation of extensive lava plains. Named after [[Hesperia Planum]].<ref name=":0" />
* [[Amazonian (Mars)|Amazonian]] period: between 3.3 and 2.9&nbsp;billion years ago to the present. Amazonian regions have few [[impact event|meteorite impact]] craters but are otherwise quite varied. [[Olympus Mons]] formed during this period, with lava flows elsewhere on Mars. Named after [[Amazonis Planitia]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Recent geological activity ===
Geological activity is still taking place on Mars. The [[Athabasca Valles]] is home to sheet-like lava flows created about 200&nbsp;million years ago. Water flows in the [[graben]]s called the [[Cerberus Fossae]] occurred less than 20&nbsp;million years ago, indicating equally recent volcanic intrusions.<ref name="ag44_4" /> The ''[[Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter]]'' has captured images of avalanches.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Russell |first=Patrick |date=3 March 2008 |title=Caught in Action: Avalanches on North Polar Scarps |url=https://hirise.lpl.arizona.edu/PSP_007338_2640 |access-date=28 March 2022 |website=HiRISE Operations Center |archive-date=7 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407233021/https://hirise.lpl.arizona.edu/PSP_007338_2640 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=12 August 2020 |title=HiRISE Catches an Avalanche on Mars |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/images/pia24035-hirise-catches-an-avalanche-on-mars |access-date=28 March 2022 |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301110525/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/images/pia24035-hirise-catches-an-avalanche-on-mars |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Physical characteristics ==
{{Main|Geology of Mars|Composition of Mars}}

[[File:Terrestrial planet size comp 2024.png|thumb|right|upright=1.4|Mars depicted to scale alongside the [[planetary-mass object]]s of the [[Inner Solar System]]. From left: [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]], [[Venus]], [[Earth]], the [[Moon]], Mars and [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]].]]

Mars is approximately half the diameter of Earth or twice that of the Moon, with a surface area only slightly less than the total area of Earth's dry land.<ref name="NasaFactSheet" /> Mars is less dense than Earth, having about 15% of Earth's volume and 11% of Earth's [[mass]], resulting in about 38% of [[Gravity of Earth|Earth's surface gravity]]. Mars is the only presently known example of a [[desert planet]], a rocky planet with a surface akin to that of Earth's [[desert]]s. The red-orange appearance of the Martian surface is caused by [[iron(III) oxide]] ([[nanophase]] Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) and the [[iron(III) oxide-hydroxide]] mineral [[goethite]].<ref name="rust" /> It can look like [[butterscotch]];<ref name="ismars" /> other common surface colors include golden, brown, tan, and greenish, depending on the [[mineral]]s present.<ref name="ismars">[http://mars.jpl.nasa.gov/msl/multimedia/videos/index.cfm?v=29&a=2 NASA – ''Mars in a Minute: Is Mars Really Red?''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140720135450/http://mars.jpl.nasa.gov/msl/multimedia/videos/index.cfm?v=29&a=2 |date=20 July 2014 }} ([http://mars.jpl.nasa.gov/multimedia/videos/movies/miam20111110/miam20111110.pdf Transcript]{{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151106174558/http://mars.jpl.nasa.gov/multimedia/videos/movies/miam20111110/miam20111110.pdf |date=6 November 2015 }}) {{PD-notice}}</ref>

=== Internal structure ===
[[File:Mars Internal Structure (2024).svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Internal structure of Mars, assuming no inner core.<ref name="Stähler"/><ref name="2023Natur.622..712S"/>]]
[[File:GMM-3 Mars Gravity.webm|thumb|Mapped gravity field of Mars]]

Like Earth, Mars is [[planetary differentiation|differentiated]] into a dense metallic [[Planetary core|core]] overlaid by less dense rocky layers.<ref name="Nimmo 2005"/><ref name="mars-in-depth"/> The outermost layer is the crust, which is on average about {{convert|42-56|km}} thick,<ref name="2023GeoRL..5003482K"/> with a minimum thickness of {{convert|6|km}} in [[Isidis Planitia]], and a maximum thickness of {{convert|117|km}} in the southern [[Tharsis|Tharsis plateau]].<ref name="2022JGRE..12707298W"/> For comparison, Earth's crust averages 27.3 ± 4.8&nbsp;km in thickness.<ref name="2013GGG....14.2003H"/> The most abundant elements in the Martian [[crust (geology)|crust]] are [[silicon]], [[oxygen]], [[iron]], [[magnesium]], [[aluminium|aluminum]], [[calcium]], and [[potassium]]. Mars is confirmed to be seismically active;<ref name="2023GeoRL..5003619F"/> in 2019, it was reported that [[InSight]] had detected and recorded over 450 [[marsquake]]s and related events.<ref name="2020NatCo..11.1014G"/><ref name="2020NatGe..13..183B"/>

Beneath the crust is a silicate [[mantle (geology)|mantle]] responsible for many of the [[Tectonics of Mars|tectonic]] and [[Volcanology of Mars|volcanic features]] on the planet's surface. The upper Martian mantle is a [[low-velocity zone]], where the velocity of seismic waves is lower than surrounding depth intervals. The mantle appears to be rigid down to the depth of about 250&nbsp;km,<ref name="2023Natur.622..712S"/> giving Mars a very thick [[lithosphere]] compared to Earth. Below this the mantle gradually becomes more ductile, and the seismic wave velocity starts to grow again.<ref name="Khan2021"/> The Martian mantle does not appear to have a thermally insulating layer analogous to Earth's [[lower mantle]]; instead, below 1050&nbsp;km in depth, it becomes mineralogically similar to Earth's [[Transition zone (Earth)|transition zone]].<ref name="Stähler"/> At the bottom of the mantle lies a basal [[magma ocean|liquid silicate layer]] approximately 150–180&nbsp;km thick.<ref name="2023Natur.622..712S"/><ref name="2023Natur.622..718K"/> The Martian mantle appears to be highly heterogenous, with dense fragments up to 4&nbsp;km across, likely injected deep into the planet by colossal impacts ~4.5 billion years ago; high-frequency waves from eight marsquakes slowed as they passed these localized regions, and modeling indicates the heterogeneities are compositionally distinct debris preserved because Mars lacks plate tectonics and has a sluggishly convecting interior that prevents complete homogenization.<ref name="Charalambous2025"/><ref>{{cite web |title=NASA Marsquake Data Reveals Lumpy Nature of Red Planet's Interior |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-marsquake-data-reveals-lumpy-nature-of-red-planets-interior/ |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |access-date=8 September 2025}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

Mars's [[iron–nickel alloy|iron and nickel]] core is at least partially molten, and may have a solid inner core.<ref name="2023Natur.619..733L"/><ref name="ArsTechnicaOn2023Natur.619..733L"/><ref name="Bi2025"/> It is around half of Mars's radius, approximately 1650–1675&nbsp;km, and is enriched in light elements such as [[sulfur]], oxygen, [[carbon]], and [[hydrogen]].<ref name="10.1038/d41586-023-03151-x"/><ref name="10.1038/d41586-023-03271-4"/> The temperature of the core is estimated to be 2000–2400&nbsp;K,<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1126/sciadv.adk1087 | title=A thermally conductive Martian core and implications for its dynamo cessation | date=2024 | journal=Science Advances | volume=10 | issue=12 | pmid=38507495 | bibcode=2024SciA...10K1087H | vauthors = Hsieh W, Deschamps F, Tsao Y, Yoshino T, Lin J | article-number=eadk1087 | pmc=10954222 }}</ref> compared to 5400–6230 K for [[Earth's inner core|Earth's solid inner core]]. Whether or not a solid inner core is present inside Mars remains a topic of active research; a 2023 study using data from the [[InSight]] lander suggested the absence of a solid inner core,<ref name="2023Natur.619..733L" /> however a 2025 study based on the same data reported the detection of a solid inner core {{convert|613|km}} ± {{convert|67|km}} in radius.<ref name="Bi2025" />

=== Surface geology ===
{{Further|Martian regolith}}
[[File:Mars 360 animation.webm|thumb|Mars 360 animation of the [[Martian surface]]]]
Mars is a [[terrestrial planet]] with a surface that consists of minerals containing [[silicon]] and oxygen, [[metal]]s, and other elements that typically make up [[rock (geology)|rock]]. The [[Martian surface]] is primarily composed of [[Tholeiitic magma series|tholeiitic]] [[basalt]],<ref name="science324_5928_736" /> although parts are more [[silica]]-rich than typical basalt and may be similar to [[andesitic]] rocks on Earth, or silica glass. Regions of low [[albedo]] suggest concentrations of [[plagioclase feldspar]], with northern low albedo regions displaying higher than normal concentrations of sheet silicates and high-silicon glass. Parts of the southern highlands include detectable amounts of high-calcium [[pyroxene]]s. Localized concentrations of [[hematite]] and [[olivine]] have been found.<ref name="jgr107_E6" /> Much of the surface is deeply covered by finely grained [[iron(III) oxide]] dust.<ref name="sci300a" />

The ''[[Phoenix (spacecraft)|Phoenix]]'' lander returned data showing Martian soil to be slightly alkaline and containing elements such as [[magnesium]], [[sodium]], [[potassium]] and [[chlorine]]. These nutrients are found in soils on Earth, and are necessary for plant growth.<ref name="bbc080627" /> Experiments performed by the lander showed that the Martian soil has a [[Base (chemistry)|basic]] [[pH]] of 7.7, and contains 0.6% [[perchlorate]] by weight,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kounaves |first1=S. P. |year=2010 |title=Wet Chemistry Experiments on the 2007 Phoenix Mars Scout Lander: Data Analysis and Results |journal=J. Geophys. Res. |volume=115 |issue=E3 |pages=E00–E10 |doi=10.1029/2008JE003084 |bibcode=2009JGRE..114.0A19K |s2cid=39418301 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kounaves |first1=S. P. |year=2010 |title=Soluble Sulfate in the Martian Soil at the Phoenix Landing Site |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=37 |issue=9 |page=L09201 |article-number=2010GL042613 |doi=10.1029/2010GL042613 |bibcode=2010GeoRL..37.9201K |s2cid=12914422}}</ref> concentrations that are [[Martian soil#Toxicity|toxic to humans]].<ref name="toxicmars">{{cite web |url=https://www.space.com/21554-mars-toxic-perchlorate-chemicals.html |title=Toxic Mars: Astronauts Must Deal with Perchlorate on the Red Planet |work=Space.com |first=Leonard |last=David |date=13 June 2013 |access-date=26 November 2018 |archive-date=20 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201120151522/https://www.space.com/21554-mars-toxic-perchlorate-chemicals.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="toxicsoil1">{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/jul/06/mars-covered-in-toxic-chemicals-that-can-wipe-out-living-organisms-tests-reveal |title=Mars covered in toxic chemicals that can wipe out living organisms, tests reveal |work=The Guardian |first=Ian |last=Sample |date=6 July 2017 |access-date=26 November 2018 |archive-date=18 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210218180154/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/jul/06/mars-covered-in-toxic-chemicals-that-can-wipe-out-living-organisms-tests-reveal |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Dark slope streak|Streaks]] are common across Mars and new ones appear frequently on steep slopes of craters, troughs, and valleys. The streaks are dark at first and get lighter with age. The streaks can start in a tiny area, then spread out for hundreds of metres. They have been seen to follow the edges of boulders and other obstacles in their path. The commonly accepted hypotheses include that they are dark underlying layers of soil revealed after avalanches of bright dust or [[dust devil]]s.<ref name="jpl_dust_devil" /> Several other explanations have been put forward, including those that involve water or even the growth of organisms.<ref name="gpl29_23_41" /><ref name="oleb33_4_515" />

[[Environmental radioactivity|Environmental radiation]] levels on the surface are on average 0.64&nbsp;[[sievert|millisieverts]] of radiation per day, and significantly less than the radiation of&nbsp;1.84&nbsp;millisieverts per day or 22&nbsp;[[Rad (radiation unit)|millirads]] per day during the flight to and from Mars.<ref name="Williams 2016">{{cite web |last=Williams |first=Matt |date=21 November 2016 |title=How bad is the radiation on Mars? |url=https://phys.org/news/2016-11-bad-mars.html |access-date=9 April 2023 |website=Phys.org |archive-date=4 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404151856/https://phys.org/news/2016-11-bad-mars.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Wall 2013">{{cite web |last=Wall |first=Mike |date=9 December 2013 |title=Radiation on Mars 'Manageable' for Manned Mission, Curiosity Rover Reveals |url=https://www.space.com/23875-mars-radiation-life-manned-mission.html |access-date=9 April 2023 |website=Space.com |archive-date=15 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201215082045/https://www.space.com/23875-mars-radiation-life-manned-mission.html |url-status=live}}</ref> For comparison the radiation levels in [[low Earth orbit]], where Earth's [[space station]]s orbit, are around 0.5&nbsp;millisieverts of radiation per day.<ref name="NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) 2003">{{cite web |date=13 March 2003 |title=Comparison of Martian Radiation Environment with International Space Station |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/images/pia04258-comparison-of-martian-radiation-environment-with-international-space-station |access-date=9 April 2023 |website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) |archive-date=9 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230409210426/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/images/pia04258-comparison-of-martian-radiation-environment-with-international-space-station |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Hellas Planitia]] has the lowest surface radiation at about 0.342 millisieverts per day, featuring [[lava tube]]s southwest of [[Hadriacus Mons]] with potentially levels as low as 0.064 millisieverts per day,<ref name="Paris Davies Tognetti Zahniser 2020">{{cite arXiv |last1=Paris |first1=Antonio |last2=Davies |first2=Evan |last3=Tognetti |first3=Laurence |last4=Zahniser |first4=Carly |date=27 April 2020 |title=Prospective Lava Tubes at Hellas Planitia |class=astro-ph.EP |eprint=2004.13156v1}}</ref> comparable to radiation levels during flights on Earth.

=== Magnetic characteristics ===
{{main|Magnetic field of Mars}}

Although Mars has no evidence of a structured [[Magnetic field of Mars|global magnetic field]],<ref name="magnetosphere" /> observations show that parts of the planet's crust have been magnetized, suggesting that alternating polarity reversals of its dipole field have occurred in the past. This [[paleomagnetism]] of magnetically susceptible minerals is similar to the [[Plate tectonics#Magnetic striping|alternating bands found on Earth's ocean floors]]. One hypothesis, published in 1999 and re-examined in October&nbsp;2005 (with the help of the ''[[Mars Global Surveyor]]''), is that these bands suggest [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonic activity]] on Mars four billion years ago, before the planetary [[Dynamo theory|dynamo]] ceased to function and the planet's magnetic field faded.<ref name="plates" />

== Geography and features ==
{{anchor|Geography}}
{{Main|Geography of Mars}}

{{further|Areoid}}
{{See also|Category:Surface features of Mars}}[[File:USGS-PlanetMars-TopographicalMap.png|thumb|upright=1.6|right|Topographical map of Mars with features labeled and the [[Martian dichotomy]] visible (northern low lying and southern highland hemispheres)]]
[[File:Mars surface map.png|thumb|[[Martian surface|Mars surface]] map rendered using a color map and a [[heightmap]] from [[NASA]]]]

Although better remembered for mapping the Moon, [[Johann Heinrich von Mädler]] and [[Wilhelm Beer]] were the first areographers. They began by establishing that most of Mars's surface features were permanent and by more precisely determining the planet's rotation period. In 1840, Mädler combined ten years of observations and drew the first map of Mars.<ref>{{cite web |date=19 October 2016 |title=What Mars Maps Got Right (and Wrong) Through Time |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/planets-maps-exploring-mars-space-science |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210221031131/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/planets-maps-exploring-mars-space-science |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 February 2021 |access-date=15 January 2022 |website=National Geographic |language=en}}</ref>

Features on Mars are named from a variety of sources. [[Classical albedo features on Mars|Albedo features]] are named for classical mythology. Craters larger than roughly 50&nbsp;km are named for deceased scientists and writers and others who have contributed to the study of Mars. Smaller craters are named for towns and villages of the world with populations of less than 100,000. Large valleys are named for the word "Mars" or "star" in various languages; smaller valleys are named for rivers.<ref name="usgs" />

Large [[albedo]] features retain many of the older names but are often updated to reflect new knowledge of the nature of the features. For example, ''Nix Olympica'' (the snows of Olympus) has become ''[[Olympus Mons]]'' (Mount Olympus).<ref name="viking_1950_2000" /> The surface of Mars as seen from Earth is divided into two kinds of areas, with differing albedo. The paler plains covered with dust and sand rich in reddish iron oxides were once thought of as Martian "continents" and given names like [[Arabia Terra]] (''land of Arabia'') or [[Amazonis Planitia]] (''Amazonian plain''). The dark features were thought to be seas, hence their names [[Mare Erythraeum]], Mare Sirenum and [[Aurorae Sinus]]. The largest dark feature seen from Earth is [[Syrtis Major Planum]].<ref>{{Citation |chapter=Syrtis Major (MC-13) |date=2019 |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/atlas-of-mars/syrtis-major-mc13/A385CD9E498305DA40E50BD83C531340 |title=The Atlas of Mars: Mapping its Geography and Geology |pages=136–139 |editor-last=Tanaka |editor-first=Kenneth L. |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/9781139567428.018 |isbn=978-1-139-56742-8 |s2cid=240843698 |access-date=18 January 2022 |editor2-last=Coles |editor2-first=Kenneth S. |editor3-last=Christensen |editor3-first=Philip R. |archive-date=1 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301160859/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/atlas-of-mars/syrtis-major-mc13/A385CD9E498305DA40E50BD83C531340 |url-status=live|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> The permanent northern polar ice cap is named [[Planum Boreum]]. The southern cap is called [[Planum Australe]].<ref name=":3" />

Mars's equator is defined by its rotation, but the location of its [[Prime Meridian]] was specified, as was Earth's (at [[Greenwich]]), by choice of an arbitrary point; Mädler and Beer selected a line for their first maps of Mars in 1830. After the spacecraft ''[[Mariner 9]]'' provided extensive imagery of Mars in 1972, a small crater (later called [[Airy-0]]), located in the [[Sinus Meridiani]] ("Middle Bay" or "Meridian Bay"), was chosen by [[Merton E. Davies]], [[Harold Masursky]], and [[Gérard de Vaucouleurs]] for the definition of 0.0° longitude to coincide with the original selection.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Davies |first1=Merton E. |last2=Berg |first2=Richard A. |date=10 January 1971 |title=A preliminary control net of Mars |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/JB076i002p00373 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |volume=76 |issue=2 |pages=373–393 |doi=10.1029/JB076i002p00373 |bibcode=1971JGR....76..373D |access-date=22 March 2022 |archive-date=1 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301160852/https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1029/JB076i002p00373 |url-status=live|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="archinal_caplinger" /><ref>{{Citation |last1=de Vaucouleurs |first1=Gerard |title=Mariner 9 Areographic Coordinate System |date=1973 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |volume=78 |issue=20 |pages=4395–4404 |bibcode=1973JGR....78.4395D |doi=10.1029/JB078i020p04395 |last2=Davies |first2=Merton E. |last3=Sturms |first3=Francis M. Jr. |author-link=Gerard de Vaucouleurs |author2-link=Merton Davies}}</ref>

Because Mars has no oceans, and hence no "[[sea level]]", a zero-elevation surface had to be selected as a reference level; this is called the ''[[areoid]]''<ref name="NASAMola2007" /> of Mars, analogous to the terrestrial [[geoid]].<ref name="ArdalanKarimi2009">{{cite journal |last1=Ardalan |first1=A. A. |last2=Karimi |first2=R. |last3=Grafarend |first3=E. W. |title=A New Reference Equipotential Surface, and Reference Ellipsoid for the Planet Mars |journal=Earth, Moon, and Planets |volume=106 |issue=1 |year=2009 |pages=1–13 |issn=0167-9295 |doi=10.1007/s11038-009-9342-7 |s2cid=119952798}}</ref> Zero altitude was defined by the height at which there is {{convert|610.5|Pa|mbar|abbr=on|lk=on}} of atmospheric pressure.<ref name="pers66" /> This pressure corresponds to the [[triple point]] of water, and it is about 0.6% of the sea level surface pressure on Earth (0.006 atm).<ref name="lunine99" />

For mapping purposes, the [[United States Geological Survey]] divides the surface of Mars into [[List of quadrangles on Mars|thirty cartographic quadrangles]], each named for a classical albedo feature it contains.<ref>{{cite web |title=ESA Science & Technology – Using iMars: Viewing Mars Express data of the MC11 quadrangle |url=https://sci.esa.int/web/mars-express/-/59473-using-imars-viewing-mars-express-data-of-the-mc11-quadrangle |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229234909/https://sci.esa.int/web/mars-express/-/59473-using-imars-viewing-mars-express-data-of-the-mc11-quadrangle |archive-date=29 December 2021 |access-date=29 December 2021 |website=sci.esa.int}}</ref> In April 2023, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported an updated global map of Mars based on images from the [[Hope Mars Mission|Hope spacecraft]].<ref name="NYT-20230415">{{cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=15 April 2023 |title=New Mars Map Lets You 'See the Whole Planet at Once' – Scientists assembled 3,000 images from an Emirati orbiter to create the prettiest atlas yet of the red planet. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/15/science/astronomy-mars-atlas.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230516125940/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/15/science/astronomy-mars-atlas.html |archive-date=16 May 2023 |access-date=15 April 2023 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> A related, but much more detailed, global Mars map was released by [[NASA]] on 16 April 2023.<ref name="STD-20230416">{{cite news |author=Staff |title=Welcome to Mars! Caltech's Jaw-Dropping, 5.7 Terapixel Virtual Expedition Across the Red Planet |url=https://scitechdaily.com/welcome-to-mars-caltechs-jaw-dropping-5-7-terapixel-virtual-expedition-across-the-red-planet/ |date=16 April 2023 |work=[[SciTech (magazine)|SciTech]] |access-date=6 April 2023 |archive-date=16 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230416204703/https://scitechdaily.com/welcome-to-mars-caltechs-jaw-dropping-5-7-terapixel-virtual-expedition-across-the-red-planet/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Volcanoes ===
{{Main|Volcanism on Mars}}

[[File:Olympus Mons - ESA Mars Express - Flickr - Andrea Luck.png|thumb|upright=1.2|Picture of the tallest volcano on Mars, [[Olympus Mons]]. It is approximately {{convert|550|km|abbr=on}} across.]]
The vast upland region [[Tharsis]] contains several massive volcanoes, which include the [[shield volcano]] [[Olympus Mons]]. The edifice is over {{convert|600|km|mi|abbr=on}} wide.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mars Atlas: Olympus Mons |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/gallery/atlas/olympus-mons.html |access-date=30 March 2022 |website=NASA's Mars Exploration Program |archive-date=29 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329181023/https://mars.nasa.gov/gallery/atlas/olympus-mons.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Plescia04">{{cite journal |last1=Plescia |first1=J. B. |year=2004 |title=Morphometric Properties of Martian Volcanoes |journal=J. Geophys. Res. |volume=109 |issue=E3 |page=E03003 |article-number=2002JE002031 |bibcode=2004JGRE..109.3003P |doi=10.1029/2002JE002031 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Because the mountain is so large, with complex structure at its edges, giving a definite height to it is difficult. Its local relief, from the foot of the cliffs which form its northwest margin to its peak, is over {{convert|21|km|mi|abbr=on}},<ref name="Plescia04" /> a little over twice the height of [[Mauna Kea]] as measured from its base on the ocean floor. The total elevation change from the plains of [[Amazonis Planitia]], over {{convert|1000|km|mi|abbr=on}} to the northwest, to the summit approaches {{convert|26|km|mi|abbr=on}},<ref name="Comins">{{cite book |last=Comins |first=Neil F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qK_4mNve1DYC&pg=PA148 |title=Discovering the Essential Universe |publisher=W. H. Freeman |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-4292-5519-6 |page=148}}</ref> roughly three times the height of [[Mount Everest]], which in comparison stands at just over {{convert|8.8|km}}. Consequently, Olympus Mons is either the [[List of tallest mountains in the Solar System|tallest or second-tallest mountain in the Solar System]]; the only known mountain which might be taller is the [[Rheasilvia]] peak on the asteroid [[4 Vesta|Vesta]], at {{convert|20-25|km|mi|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Schenk2012">{{cite journal |last1=Schenk |first1=P. |date=2012 |title=The Geologically Recent Giant Impact Basins at Vesta's South Pole |journal=Science |volume=336 |issue=6082 |pages=694–697 |bibcode=2012Sci...336..694S |doi=10.1126/science.1223272 |pmid=22582256 |s2cid=206541950}}</ref>

=== Impact topography ===
The [[Martian dichotomy|dichotomy of Martian topography]] is striking: northern plains flattened by lava flows contrast with the southern highlands, pitted and cratered by ancient impacts. It is possible that, four billion years ago, the Northern Hemisphere of Mars was struck by an object one-tenth to two-thirds the size of Earth's [[Moon]]. If this is the case, the Northern Hemisphere of Mars would be the site of an [[impact crater]] {{convert|10600|by|8500|km}} in size, or roughly the area of Europe, Asia, and Australia combined, surpassing [[Utopia Planitia]] and the Moon's [[South Pole–Aitken basin]] as the largest impact crater in the Solar System.<ref>{{cite journal |title=The Borealis basin and the origin of the Martian crustal dichotomy |last1=Andrews-Hanna |first1=Jeffrey C. |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=453 |pages=1212–1215 |doi=10.1038/nature07011 |year=2008 |pmid=18580944 |last2=Zuber |first2=Maria T. |author-link2=Maria Zuber |last3=Banerdt |first3=W. Bruce |issue=7199 |bibcode=2008Natur.453.1212A |s2cid=1981671}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{cite web |last=Choi |first=Charles |date=1 October 2021 |title=Mars: What We Know About the Red Planet |url=https://www.space.com/47-mars-the-red-planet-fourth-planet-from-the-sun.html |access-date=6 January 2022 |website=Space.com |language=en |archive-date=6 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220106100851/https://www.space.com/47-mars-the-red-planet-fourth-planet-from-the-sun.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Moskowitz |first=Clara |date=25 June 2008 |title=Huge Impact Created Mars' Split Personality |url=https://www.space.com/5558-huge-impact-created-mars-split-personality.html |access-date=6 January 2022 |website=Space.com |language=en |archive-date=6 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220106102110/https://www.space.com/5558-huge-impact-created-mars-split-personality.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

Mars is scarred by 43,000 impact craters with a diameter of {{convert|5|km}} or greater.<ref name="wright03" /> The largest exposed crater is [[Hellas Planitia|Hellas]], which is {{convert|2300|km}} wide and {{convert|7000|m|ft}} deep, and is a light [[albedo feature]] clearly visible from Earth.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vogt |first=Gregory L. |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-0-387-75468-0_2.pdf |title=Landscapes of Mars |date=2008 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-75467-3 |location=New York, NY |pages=44 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-75468-0 |access-date=31 March 2022 |archive-date=1 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301160105/https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-0-387-75468-0_2 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=ESA Science & Technology – Craters within the Hellas Basin |url=https://sci.esa.int/web/mars-express/-/55575-craters-within-the-hellas-basin |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220102121425/https://sci.esa.int/web/mars-express/-/55575-craters-within-the-hellas-basin |archive-date=2 January 2022 |access-date=2 January 2022 |website=sci.esa.int}}</ref> There are other notable impact features, such as [[Argyre Planitia|Argyre]], which is around {{convert|1800|km}} in diameter,<ref>{{cite web |first=Christine M. |last=Rodrigue |url=https://home.csulb.edu/~rodrigue/mars/FNlecture.html |title=The Geography of Mars |publisher=Home.csulb.edu |date= |access-date=20 February 2022 |archive-date=30 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220130013414/https://home.csulb.edu/~rodrigue/mars/FNlecture.html |url-status=live}}</ref> and [[Isidis Planitia|Isidis]], which is around {{convert|1500|km}} in diameter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=41st Lunar and Planetary Science Conference (2010) |url=https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2010/pdf/1294.pdf |access-date=31 January 2022 |archive-date=30 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220130215730/https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2010/pdf/1294.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> Due to the smaller mass and size of Mars, the probability of an object colliding with the planet is about half that of Earth. Mars is located closer to the [[asteroid belt]], so it has an increased chance of being struck by materials from that source. Mars is more likely to be struck by short-period [[comet]]s, ''i.e.'', those that lie within the orbit of [[Jupiter]].<ref name="emp9" />

Martian craters can{{discuss}} have a morphology that suggests the ground became wet after the meteor impact.<ref name="emp45" />

=== Tectonic sites ===
[[File:PlanetMars-VallesMarineris-VikingOrbiter-1980.jpg|thumb|[[Valles Marineris]], taken by the ''[[Viking 1]]'' probe]]
The large canyon, [[Valles Marineris]] (Latin for [[Mariner program|Mariner]] Valleys, also known as Agathodaemon in the old canal maps<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sagan |first1=Carl |author-link=Carl Sagan |last2=Fox |first2=Paul |date=August 1975 |title=The canals of Mars: An assessment after Mariner 9 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0019103575900421 |journal=Icarus |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=602–612 |doi=10.1016/0019-1035(75)90042-1 |bibcode=1975Icar...25..602S |access-date=22 March 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>), has a length of {{convert|4000|km}} and a depth of up to {{convert|7|km}}. The length of Valles Marineris is equivalent to the length of Europe and extends across one-fifth the circumference of Mars. By comparison, the [[Grand Canyon]] on Earth is only {{convert|446|km}} long and nearly {{convert|2|km}} deep. Valles Marineris was formed due to the swelling of the Tharsis area, which caused the crust in the area of Valles Marineris to collapse. In 2012, it was proposed that Valles Marineris is not just a [[graben]], but a plate boundary where {{convert|150|km}} of [[Transform fault|transverse motion]] has occurred, making Mars a planet with possibly a two-[[tectonic plate]] arrangement.<ref name="tectonic">{{cite web |url=http://newsroom.ucla.edu/portal/ucla/ucla-scientist-discovers-plate-237303.aspx |title=UCLA scientist discovers plate tectonics on Mars |publisher=UCLA |date=9 August 2012 |access-date=13 August 2012 |last=Wolpert |first=Stuart |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120812215548/http://newsroom.ucla.edu/portal/ucla/ucla-scientist-discovers-plate-237303.aspx |archive-date=12 August 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Lin, An">{{cite journal |last=Lin |first=An |title=Structural analysis of the Valles Marineris fault zone: Possible evidence for large-scale strike-slip faulting on Mars |journal=Lithosphere |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=286–330 |date=4 June 2012 |doi=10.1130/L192.1 |bibcode=2012Lsphe...4..286Y |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Holes and caves ===
Images from the [[Thermal Emission Imaging System]] (THEMIS) aboard NASA's [[2001 Mars Odyssey|Mars Odyssey orbiter]] have revealed seven possible [[cave]] entrances on the flanks of the volcano [[Arsia Mons]].<ref name="cushing_titus_wynn07" /> The caves, named after loved ones of their discoverers, are collectively known as the "seven sisters".<ref name="nau070328" /> Cave entrances measure from {{convert|100|to|252|m}} wide and they are estimated to be at least {{convert|73|to|96|m}} deep. Because light does not reach the floor of most of the caves, they may extend much deeper than these lower estimates and widen below the surface. "Dena" is the only exception; its floor is visible and was measured to be {{convert|130|m}} deep. The interiors of these caverns may be protected from micrometeoroids, UV radiation, [[solar flare]]s and high energy particles that bombard the planet's surface.<ref name="bbc070317" /><ref>{{cite web |title=The Caves of Mars {{!}} U.S. Geological Survey |url=https://www.usgs.gov/news/caves-mars |access-date=12 January 2022 |publisher=USGS |archive-date=31 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211231032913/http://www.usgs.gov/news/caves-mars |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Atmosphere ==
{{Main|Atmosphere of Mars}}

[[File:Mars - Atmosphere and Cassini Crater - Hope Mission, Orbit 19 (52252929420).png|alt=Image of Mars|thumb|A broad view of Mars's atmosphere by ''Hope'' orbiter.]]
Mars lost its [[magnetosphere]] 4&nbsp;billion years ago,<ref name="swind" /> possibly because of numerous asteroid strikes,<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.wired.com/2011/01/mars-dynamo-death/ |title=Multiple Asteroid Strikes May Have Killed Mars's Magnetic Field |date=20 January 2011 |access-date=30 March 2022 |magazine=Wired |last1=Grossman |first1=Lisa |archive-date=30 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230034219/http://www.wired.com/wiredscience/2011/01/mars-dynamo-death/ |url-status=live}}</ref> so the [[solar wind]] interacts directly with the Martian [[ionosphere]], lowering the atmospheric density by [[atmospheric stripping|stripping]] away atoms from the outer layer.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Jakosky |first=Bruce M. |date=1 April 2022 |title=How did Mars lose its atmosphere and water? |journal=Physics Today |volume=75 |issue=4 |pages=62–63 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.4988 |bibcode=2022PhT....75d..62J |s2cid=247882540 |issn=0031-9228 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Both ''[[Mars Global Surveyor]]'' and ''[[Mars Express]]'' have detected ionized atmospheric particles trailing off into space behind Mars,<ref name="swind" /><ref name="swind2" /> and this atmospheric loss is being studied by the [[MAVEN]] orbiter. Compared to Earth, the [[celestial body atmosphere|atmosphere]] of Mars is quite rarefied. [[Atmospheric pressure]] on the surface today ranges from a low of {{convert|30|Pa|psi|abbr=on|lk=on}} on [[Olympus Mons]] to over {{convert|1155|Pa|psi|abbr=on}} in [[Hellas Planitia]], with a mean pressure at the surface level of {{convert|600|Pa|psi|abbr=on}}.<ref name="bolonkin09" /> The highest atmospheric density on Mars is equal to that found {{convert|35|km}}<ref name="atkinson07" /> above Earth's surface. The resulting mean surface pressure is only 0.6% of Earth's {{convert|101.3|kPa|psi|abbr=on}}. The [[scale height]] of the atmosphere is about {{convert|10.8|km}},<ref name="carr06" /> which is higher than Earth's {{convert|6|km}}, because the surface [[gravity of Mars]] is only about 38% of Earth's.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mars Facts {{!}} All About Mars |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/all-about-mars/facts |access-date=27 December 2021 |website=NASA's Mars Exploration Program |date=10 November 2017 |language=en |archive-date=10 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231010080933/https://mars.nasa.gov/all-about-mars/facts/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

The atmosphere of Mars consists of about 96% [[carbon dioxide]], 1.93% [[argon]] and 1.89% [[nitrogen]] along with traces of [[oxygen]] and water.<ref name="NasaFactSheet" /><ref name="Abundance">{{cite journal |title=Abundance and Isotopic Composition of Gases in the Martian Atmosphere from the Curiosity Rover |volume=341 |issue=6143 |pages=263–266 |journal=Science |date=19 July 2013 |doi=10.1126/science.1237966 |pmid=23869014 |last1=Mahaffy |first1=P. R. |bibcode=2013Sci...341..263M |s2cid=206548973}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> The atmosphere is quite dusty, containing particulates about 1.5 [[μm]] in diameter which give the [[Extraterrestrial skies#Mars|Martian sky]] a [[tawny (color)|tawny]] color when seen from the surface.<ref name="dusty" /> It may take on a [[pink]] hue due to [[iron oxide]] particles suspended in it.<ref name="Rees2012" />

Despite repeated detections of [[methane on Mars]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shekhtman |first=Lonnie |date=22 April 2024 |title=Why is Methane Seeping on Mars? NASA Scientists Have New Ideas – NASA Science |work=NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/why-is-methane-seeping-on-mars-nasa-scientists-have-new-ideas/ |access-date=1 January 2026 |language=en-US}}</ref> there is no scientific consensus as to its origin.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sutter |first=Paul |date=16 November 2024 |title=What's Behind the Martian Methane Mystery? |url=https://www.universetoday.com/articles/whats-behind-the-martian-methane-mystery |access-date=1 January 2026 |website=Universe Today |language=en}}</ref> One suggestion is that methane exists on Mars and that its concentration fluctuates seasonally.<ref name="Sample2018">{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2018/jun/07/nasa-mars-rover-finds-organic-matter-in-ancient-lake-bed |title=Nasa Mars rover finds organic matter in ancient lake bed |work=The Guardian |first=Ian |last=Sample |date=7 June 2018 |access-date=12 June 2018 |archive-date=18 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180618030502/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2018/jun/07/nasa-mars-rover-finds-organic-matter-in-ancient-lake-bed |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="plumes" /><ref name="nature460" /> The existence of methane could be produced by non-biological process such as [[serpentinite|serpentinization]] involving water, carbon dioxide, and the mineral [[olivine]], which is known to be common on Mars, or by Martian life.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Chang |first=Kenneth |date=1 April 2019 |title=Something on Mars Is Producing Gas Usually Made by Living Things on Earth |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/01/science/mars-methane-gas.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190401190931/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/01/science/mars-methane-gas.html |archive-date=1 April 2019 |access-date=1 January 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en}}</ref><ref name="olivine" />[[File:PIA18613-MarsMAVEN-Atmosphere-3UV-Views-20141014.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|[[Atmosphere of Mars|Escaping atmosphere]] on Mars ([[carbon]], [[oxygen]], and [[hydrogen]]) by [[MAVEN]] in [[Ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy|UV]]<ref name="NASA-20141014-NJ">{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=Nancy |last2=Steigerwald |first2=Bill |last3=Brown |first3=Dwayne |last4=Webster |first4=Guy |date=14 October 2014 |title=NASA Mission Provides Its First Look at Martian Upper Atmosphere |url=http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?release=2014-351 |access-date=15 October 2014 |publisher=NASA |archive-date=19 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141019184946/http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?release=2014-351 |url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>|300x300px]]

Compared to Earth, its higher concentration of atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> and lower surface pressure may be why sound is attenuated more on Mars, where natural sources are rare apart from the wind. Using acoustic recordings collected by the ''Perseverance'' rover, researchers concluded that the speed of sound there is approximately 240&nbsp;m/s for frequencies below 240&nbsp;Hz, and 250&nbsp;m/s for those above.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wright |first=Katherine |date=22 March 2022 |title=Sound Speed Measured on Mars |url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v15/43 |journal=[[Physics (magazine)|Physics]] |volume=15 |article-number=43 |doi=10.1103/Physics.15.43 |bibcode=2022PhyOJ..15...43W |s2cid=247720720 |doi-access=free |access-date=6 April 2022 |archive-date=12 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220412151942/https://physics.aps.org/articles/v15/43 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maurice |first1=S. |last2=Chide |first2=B. |last3=Murdoch |first3=N. |last4=Lorenz |first4=R. D. |last5=Mimoun |first5=D. |last6=Wiens |first6=R. C. |last7=Stott |first7=A. |last8=Jacob |first8=X. |last9=Bertrand |first9=T. |last10=Montmessin |first10=F. |last11=Lanza |first11=N. L. |date=1 April 2022 |title=In situ recording of Mars soundscape |journal=Nature |volume=605 |issue=7911 |pages=653–658 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-04679-0 |pmid=35364602 |pmc=9132769 |bibcode=2022Natur.605..653M |s2cid=247865804 |issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

[[Aurora on Mars|Aurora]]s have been detected on Mars.<ref>{{cite web |title=In an ultraviolet glow, auroras on Mars spotted by UAE orbiter |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/science/space/ultraviolet-glow-auroras-mars-spotted-uae-orbiter-rcna1356 |first=Denise |last=Chow |access-date=7 December 2021 |date=7 December 2021 |website=NBC News |language=en |archive-date=7 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207221852/https://www.nbcnews.com/science/space/ultraviolet-glow-auroras-mars-spotted-uae-orbiter-rcna1356 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Auroras on Mars – NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2015/11may_aurorasonmars/ |website=science.nasa.gov |date=10 May 2015 |access-date=12 May 2015 |archive-date=14 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150514060513/http://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2015/11may_aurorasonmars/ |url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref><ref name="NASA-20150318">{{cite web |last1=Brown |first1=Dwayne |last2=Neal-Jones |first2=Nancy |last3=Steigerwald |first3=Bill |last4=Scott |first4=Jim |url=http://www.nasa.gov/press/2015/march/nasa-spacecraft-detects-aurora-and-mysterious-dust-cloud-around-mars |title=NASA Spacecraft Detects Aurora and Mysterious Dust Cloud around Mars |publisher=NASA |id=Release 15-045 |date=18 March 2015 |access-date=18 March 2015 |archive-date=19 March 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150319152358/http://www.nasa.gov/press/2015/march/nasa-spacecraft-detects-aurora-and-mysterious-dust-cloud-around-mars/ |url-status=live}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> Because Mars lacks a global magnetic field, the types and distribution of auroras there differ from those on Earth;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Deighan |first1=J. |last2=Jain |first2=S. K. |last3=Chaffin |first3=M. S. |last4=Fang |first4=X. |last5=Halekas |first5=J. S. |last6=Clarke |first6=J. T. |last7=Schneider |first7=N. M. |last8=Stewart |first8=A. I. F. |last9=Chaufray |first9=J.-Y. |last10=Evans |first10=J. S. |last11=Stevens |first11=M. H. |date=October 2018 |title=Discovery of a proton aurora at Mars |url=http://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-018-0538-5 |journal=Nature Astronomy |volume=2 |issue=10 |pages=802–807 |doi=10.1038/s41550-018-0538-5 |bibcode=2018NatAs...2..802D |s2cid=105560692 |issn=2397-3366 |access-date=5 April 2022 |archive-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220522145256/https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-018-0538-5 |url-status=live}}</ref> rather than being mostly restricted to polar regions as is the case on Earth, a Martian aurora can encompass the planet.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Schneider |first1=N. M. |last2=Jain |first2=S. K. |last3=Deighan |first3=J. |last4=Nasr |first4=C. R. |last5=Brain |first5=D. A. |last6=Larson |first6=D. |last7=Lillis |first7=R. |last8=Rahmati |first8=Ali |last9=Halekas |first9=J. S. |last10=Lee |first10=C. O. |last11=Chaffin |first11=M. S. |date=16 August 2018 |title=Global Aurora on Mars During the September 2017 Space Weather Event |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=45 |issue=15 |pages=7391–7398 |doi=10.1029/2018GL077772 |bibcode=2018GeoRL..45.7391S |s2cid=115149852 |doi-access=free |hdl=10150/631256 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> In September 2017, NASA reported [[radiation]] levels on the surface of the planet Mars were temporarily [[Orders of magnitude (radiation)|doubled]], and were associated with an [[aurora]] 25 times brighter than any observed earlier, due to a massive, and unexpected, [[Coronal mass ejection|solar storm]] in the middle of the month.<ref name=":8" /><ref name="nasa20170929">{{cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/jpl/large-solar-storm-sparks-global-aurora-and-doubles-radiation-levels-on-the-martian-surface |title=Large Solar Storm Sparks Global Aurora and Doubles Radiation Levels on the Martian Surface |publisher=NASA |first1=Guy |last1=Webster |first2=Nancy |last2=Neal-Jones |first3=Jim |last3=Scott |first4=Deb |last4=Schmid |first5=Laurie |last5=Cantillo |first6=Dwayne |last6=Brown |date=29 September 2017 |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=1 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171001181055/https://www.nasa.gov/feature/jpl/large-solar-storm-sparks-global-aurora-and-doubles-radiation-levels-on-the-martian-surface/ |url-status=dead}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

=== Climate ===
{{Main|Climate of Mars}}
[[File:Mars duststorm-no text.jpg|thumb|Mars without (on left) and with a global dust storm in July 2001 (on right), including different visible water ice cloud covers, as seen by the Hubble Space Telescope.]]
[[File:PIA22546-Mars-AnnualCO2ice-N&SPoles-20180806.gif|thumb|Rendering of the change of [[dry ice|CO<sub>2</sub> ice]] (not water ice) coverage on the north (left) and south (right) poles of Mars between northern and southern summer.]]
Mars has seasons, alternating between its northern and southern hemispheres, similar to on Earth. Additionally the orbit of Mars has, compared to Earth's, a large [[Orbital eccentricity|eccentricity]] and approaches [[Apsis|perihelion]] when it is summer in its southern hemisphere and winter in its northern, and aphelion when it is winter in its southern hemisphere and summer in its northern. As a result, the seasons in its southern hemisphere are more extreme and the seasons in its northern are milder than would otherwise be the case. The summer temperatures in the south can be warmer than the equivalent summer temperatures in the north by up to {{convert|30|C-change}}.<ref name="goodman97" />

Martian surface temperatures vary from lows of about {{convert|-110|C|F}} to highs of up to {{convert|35|C|F}} in equatorial summer.<ref name="hot" /> The wide range in temperatures is due to the thin atmosphere which cannot store much solar heat, the low atmospheric pressure (about 1% that of the [[atmosphere of Earth]]), and the low [[thermal inertia]] of Martian soil.<ref name="nasa_surface" /> The planet is 1.52 times as far from the Sun as Earth, resulting in just 43% of the amount of sunlight.<ref name="disc920901" /><ref>{{cite web |last=Hille |first=Karl |date=18 September 2015 |title=The Fact and Fiction of Martian Dust Storms |url=http://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/the-fact-and-fiction-of-martian-dust-storms |access-date=25 December 2021 |website=NASA |archive-date=2 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160302231423/http://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/the-fact-and-fiction-of-martian-dust-storms/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Mars has the largest [[dust storm]]s in the Solar System, reaching speeds of over {{convert|100|mph|km/h|order=flip|abbr=on}}. These can vary from a storm over a small area, to gigantic storms that cover the entire planet. They tend to occur when Mars is closest to the Sun, and have been shown to increase global temperature.<ref name="philips01" /> Seasons also produce [[dry ice]] covering [[Martian polar ice caps|polar ice caps]].<ref name="a652">{{cite web | title=Dry Ice on Mars | website=NASA Science | date=6 April 2011 | url=https://science.nasa.gov/resource/dry-ice-on-mars/ | access-date=1 May 2025}}</ref>

== Hydrology ==
{{Main|Water on Mars}}

{{See also|Groundwater on Mars}}
[[File:PIA26046-Mars-BuriedIceMaps-20231026.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|Mars contains water, though mostly as dust covered polar layers of ice, as mapped in this image.]]

While Mars contains [[Water on terrestrial planets of the Solar System|water in larger amounts]], most of it is dust covered water ice at the [[Martian polar ice caps]].<ref name="specials1" /><ref name="bbc040124" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Holt |first1=John W. |last2=Safaeinili |first2=Ali |last3=Plaut |first3=Jeffrey J. |last4=Head |first4=James W. |last5=Phillips |first5=Roger J. |last6=Seu |first6=Roberto |last7=Kempf |first7=Scott D. |last8=Choudhary |first8=Prateek |last9=Young |first9=Duncan A. |last10=Putzig |first10=Nathaniel E. |last11=Biccari |first11=Daniela |date=21 November 2008 |title=Radar Sounding Evidence for Buried Glaciers in the Southern Mid-Latitudes of Mars |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1164246 |journal=Science |volume=322 |issue=5905 |pages=1235–1238 |bibcode=2008Sci...322.1235H |doi=10.1126/science.1164246 |issn=0036-8075 |jstor=20145331 |pmid=19023078 |s2cid=36614186 |hdl=11573/67950 |access-date=22 April 2022 |archive-date=22 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220422162701/https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1164246 |url-status=live|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="sci299" /><ref name=":3">{{cite web |title=Polar Caps |url=https://marsed.asu.edu/mep/ice/polar-caps |access-date=6 January 2022 |website=Mars Education at Arizona State University |archive-date=28 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210528133135/https://marsed.asu.edu/mep/ice/polar-caps |url-status=live}}</ref>
The volume of water ice in the south polar ice cap, if melted, would be enough to cover most of the surface of the planet with a depth of {{convert|11|m}}.<ref name="nasa070315" />

Water in its liquid form cannot persist on the surface due to Mars's low atmospheric pressure, which is less than 1% that of Earth.<ref name="nasa.gov">{{cite web |title=NASA – NASA Rover Finds Clues to Changes in Mars' Atmosphere |url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/msl/news/msl20121102.html |publisher=NASA |access-date=19 October 2014 |archive-date=26 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226060801/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/msl/news/msl20121102.html%20 |url-status=dead}} {{PD-notice}}</ref> Only at the lowest of elevations are the pressure and temperature high enough for liquid water to exist for short periods.<ref name="mars-in-depth" /><ref name="jgr110" />

Although little water is present in the atmosphere, there is enough to produce clouds of water ice and different cases of [[snow]] and frost, often mixed with snow of [[carbon dioxide]] [[dry ice]].<ref name="k104">{{cite web | title=Carbon-Dioxide Snowfall on Mars | website=NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) | date=11 September 2012 | url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/images/pia16138-carbon-dioxide-snowfall-on-mars/ | access-date=19 April 2025}}</ref>

===Past hydrosphere===
[[File:Artist’s impression of Mars four billion years ago.jpg|thumb|Artist's impression of Mars four billion years ago]]
[[Geomorphology|Landforms]] visible on Mars strongly suggest that liquid water has existed on the planet's surface. Huge linear swathes of scoured ground, known as [[outflow channels]], cut across the surface in about 25 places. These are thought to be a record of erosion caused by the catastrophic release of water from subsurface aquifers, though some of these structures have been hypothesized to result from the action of glaciers or lava.<ref name="Kerr2005" /><ref name="Jaeger2007" /> One of the larger examples, [[Ma'adim Vallis]], is {{convert|700|km}} long, much greater than the Grand Canyon, with a width of {{convert|20|km}} and a depth of {{convert|2|km}} in places. It is thought to have been carved by flowing water early in Mars's history.<ref name="lucchita_rosanova" /> The youngest of these channels is thought to have formed only a few million years ago.<ref name="nature434" />

Elsewhere, particularly on the oldest areas of the Martian surface, finer-scale, dendritic [[Valley networks (Mars)|networks of valleys]] are spread across significant proportions of the landscape. Features of these valleys and their distribution strongly imply that they were carved by [[surface runoff|runoff]] resulting from precipitation in early Mars history. Subsurface water flow and [[groundwater sapping]] may play important subsidiary roles in some networks, but precipitation was probably the root cause of the incision in almost all cases.<ref name="CraddockHoward2002" />

Along craters and canyon walls, there are thousands of features that appear similar to terrestrial [[gullies]]. The gullies tend to be in the highlands of the Southern Hemisphere and face the Equator; all are poleward of 30° latitude. A number of authors have suggested that their formation process involves liquid water, probably from melting ice,<ref name="sci288" /><ref name="nasa061206" /> although others have argued for formation mechanisms involving carbon dioxide frost or the movement of dry dust.<ref name="bbc061206" /><ref name="nasa061206b" /> No partially degraded gullies have formed by weathering and no superimposed impact craters have been observed, indicating that these are young features, possibly still active.<ref name="nasa061206" /> Other geological features, such as [[River delta|deltas]] and [[alluvial fan]]s preserved in craters, are further evidence for warmer, wetter conditions at an interval or intervals in earlier Mars history.<ref name="Lewis2006" /> Such conditions necessarily require the widespread presence of [[Volcanic crater lake|crater lakes]] across a large proportion of the surface, for which there is independent mineralogical, sedimentological and geomorphological evidence.<ref name="Matsubara2011" /> Further evidence that liquid water once existed on the surface of Mars comes from the detection of specific minerals such as [[hematite]] and [[goethite]], both of which sometimes form in the presence of water.<ref name="nasa040303" />

=== History of observations and findings of water evidence ===
{{Main|Water on Mars|Chronology of discoveries of water on Mars}}

[[File:Perspective view of Korolev crater.jpg|thumb|As top surface layer water appears readily visible at some places on Mars, as in this polar [[Korolev (Martian crater)|crater called Korolev]], seen here in [[3D projection]].]]
The chemical signature of water vapor on Mars was first unequivocally demonstrated in 1963 by spectroscopy using an Earth-based telescope.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jakosky |first1=Bruce M. |last2=Mellon |first2=Michael T. |date=1 April 2004 |title=Special Issue: Water on Mars |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/special-issue-water-on-mars |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=57 |issue=4 |pages=71–76 |doi=10.1063/1.1752425 |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=https://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1963ApJ...137.1319S | bibcode=1963ApJ...137.1319S | title=Letter to the Editor: The Detection of Water Vapor on Mars | last1=Spinrad | first1=Hyron | last2=Münch | first2=Guido | last3=Kaplan | first3=Lewis D. | journal=The Astrophysical Journal | date=1963 | volume=137 | page=1319 | doi=10.1086/147613 }}</ref> In 2004, ''Opportunity'' detected the mineral [[jarosite]]. This forms only in the presence of acidic water, showing that water once existed on Mars.<ref name="nasa101001" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elwood Madden |first1=M. E. |last2=Bodnar |first2=R. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303070003/https://www.nature.com/articles/nature02971 |url-status=live|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The ''Spirit'' rover found concentrated deposits of [[silica]] in 2007 that indicated wet conditions in the past, and in December 2011, the mineral [[gypsum]], which also forms in the presence of water, was found on the surface by NASA's Mars rover Opportunity.<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 December 2007 |title=Mars Rover Investigates Signs of Steamy Martian Past |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/mars-rover-investigates-signs-of-steamy-martian-past
