|last9=Gericke |first9=D.O. |last10=Glenzer |first10=S.H. |last11=Granados |first11=E. |last12=MacDonald |first12=M.J. |last13=MacKinnon |first13=A.J. |last14=McBride |first14=E.E. |last15=Nam |first15=I. |last16=Neumayer |first16=P. |last17=Roth |first17=M. |last18=Saunders |first18=A.M. |last19=Schuster |first19=A.K. |last20=Sun |first20=P. |last21=van Driel |first21=T. |last22=Döppner |first22=T. |last23=Falcone |first23=R.W. |display-authors=1 |volume=1 |issue=9 |pages=606–11 |date=September 2017 |doi=10.1038/s41550-017-0219-9 |bibcode=2017NatAs...1..606K |osti=1393331 }}</ref> Scientists believe that this kind of diamond rain occurs on Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kane |first=Sean |date=29 April 2016 |title=Lightning storms make it rain diamonds on Saturn and Jupiter |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/diamond-rain-saturn-jupiter-2016-4 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190626211704/https://www.businessinsider.com/diamond-rain-saturn-jupiter-2016-4 |archive-date=26 June 2019 |access-date=22 May 2019 |publisher=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref><ref name="WP-20170825"/> High-pressure experiments at [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] suggest that the top of the mantle may be an ocean of liquid carbon with floating solid 'diamonds'.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.astronomynow.com/news/n1001/21diamond/ |title=Oceans of diamond possible on Uranus and Neptune |website=Astronomy Now |first=Emily |last=Baldwin |date=21 January 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203065217/http://www.astronomynow.com/news/n1001/21diamond/ |archive-date=3 December 2013}}</ref><ref name="Eggert 2004">{{cite journal |title=Shock Compressing Diamond to a Conducting Fluid |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.93.195506 |pmid=15600850 |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=30 July 2004 |last1=Bradley |first1=D.K. |last2=Eggert |first2=J.H. |last3=Hicks |first3=D.G. |last4=Celliers |first4=P.M. |volume=93 |issue=19 |article-number=195506 |bibcode=2004PhRvL..93s5506B |hdl=1959.3/380076 }}</ref><ref name="Eggert 2010">{{cite journal |title=Melting temperature of diamond at ultrahigh pressure |journal=Nature Physics |date=8 November 2009 |last1=Eggert |first1=J.H. |last2=Hicks |first2=D.G. |last3=Celliers |first3=P.M. |last4=Bradley |first4=D.K. |volume=6 |issue=40 |pages=40–43 |doi=10.1038/nphys1438 |display-authors=etal |bibcode=2010NatPh...6...40E|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The [[planetary core|core]] of Neptune is likely composed of iron, nickel and [[silicate]]s, with an interior [[Scientific model|model]] giving a mass about 1.2x that of Earth.<ref name="Podolak Weizman et al. 1995" /> The pressure at the centre is 7&nbsp;[[bar (unit)|Mbar]] (700&nbsp;GPa), about twice as high as that at the centre of Earth, and the temperature may be {{cvt|5400|K|C F|-2}}.<ref name=hubbard/><ref name="nettelmann">{{Cite web |last1=Nettelmann |first1=N. |last2=French |first2=M. |last3=Holst |first3=B. |last4=Redmer |first4=R. |title=Interior Models of Jupiter, Saturn and Neptune |url=https://www.gsi.de/informationen/wti/library/plasma2006/PAPERS/TT-11.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718120920/https://www.gsi.de/informationen/wti/library/plasma2006/PAPERS/TT-11.pdf |archive-date=18 July 2011 |access-date=25 February 2008 |publisher=University of Rostock}}</ref>

=== Internal heating ===
Neptune's more varied weather when compared to Uranus is due in part to its higher [[internal heating]]. The upper regions of Neptune's troposphere reach a low temperature of {{cvt|51.8|K|C}}. At a depth where the [[atmospheric pressure]] equals {{Cvt|1|bar|kPa|lk=on}}, the temperature is {{cvt|72.00|K|C}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lindal |first=Gunnar F. |title=The atmosphere of Neptune&nbsp;– an analysis of radio occultation data acquired with Voyager 2 |journal=Astronomical Journal |date=1992 |volume=103 |pages=967–82 |bibcode=1992AJ....103..967L |doi=10.1086/116119|doi-access=free }}</ref> Deeper inside the layers of gas, the temperature rises steadily. As with Uranus, the source of this heating is unknown, but the discrepancy is larger: Uranus only radiates 1.1 times as much energy as it receives from the Sun;<ref>{{cite web |title=Class 12&nbsp;– Giant Planets&nbsp;– Heat and Formation |website=3750&nbsp;– Planets, Moons & Rings |date=2004 |publisher=Colorado University, Boulder |url=http://lasp.colorado.edu/~bagenal/3750/ClassNotes/Class12/Class12.html |access-date=13 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080621120100/http://lasp.colorado.edu/~bagenal/3750/ClassNotes/Class12/Class12.html |archive-date=21 June 2008 |url-status=live }}{{self-published inline|date=March 2026}}</ref> whereas Neptune radiates about 2.61 times as much energy as it receives from the Sun.<ref name="Pearl_et_al_Neptune" />

Neptune is over 50% farther from the Sun than Uranus and receives only ~40% of Uranus's amount of sunlight;<ref name="Lunine 1993" /> however, its [[internal energy]] is still enough for the fastest planetary winds in the Solar System. Depending on the thermal properties of its interior, the heat left over from Neptune's formation may be sufficient to explain its current heat flow, though it is harder to explain Uranus's lack of internal heat while preserving the apparent similarity between the two planets.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Pater |first1=Imke de |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RaJdy3_VINQC&dq=planet+neptune+heat+flow&pg=PA224 |title=Planetary Sciences |last2=Lissauer |first2=Jack J. |date=6 December 2001 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-48219-6 |page=224 |access-date=15 March 2023 |archive-date=29 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210929080319/https://books.google.com/books?id=RaJdy3_VINQC&pg=PA224&lpg=PA224&dq=planet+neptune+heat+flow |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Rotation and magnetosphere==
=== Rotation ===
The [[axial tilt]] of Neptune is 28.32°,<ref>{{cite web |last=Williams |first=David R. |date=6 January 2005 |url=http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/planetfact.html |title=Planetary Fact Sheets |publisher=NASA |access-date=28 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080925071832/http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/planetfact.html |archive-date=25 September 2008 |url-status=live }}</ref> which is similar to the tilts of Earth (23°) and Mars (25°). As a result, Neptune experiences seasonal changes similar to those on Earth. The long [[orbital period]] of Neptune means that the seasons last for forty Earth years.<ref name=villard/> Its sidereal rotation period (day) is roughly 16.11&nbsp;hours.<ref name="fact2" /> Because its axial tilt is comparable to Earth's, the variation in the length of its day over the course of its long year is not any more extreme.

Because Neptune is not a solid body, its atmosphere undergoes [[differential rotation]]. The wide equatorial zone rotates with a period of about 18&nbsp;hours, which is slower than the 16.1-hour rotation of the planet's magnetic field. By contrast, the reverse is true for the polar regions where the rotation period is 12&nbsp;hours. This differential rotation is the most pronounced of any planet in the Solar System,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hubbard |first1=W. B. |last2=Nellis |first2=W. J. |last3=Mitchell |first3=A. C. |last4=Holmes |first4=N. C. |last5=Limaye |first5=S. S. |last6=McCandless |first6=P. C. |display-authors=4 |date=9 August 1991 |title=Interior Structure of Neptune: Comparison with Uranus |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1231004 |url-status=live |journal=Science |volume=253 |issue=5020 |pages=648–651 |bibcode=1991Sci...253..648H |doi=10.1126/science.253.5020.648 |pmid=17772369 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181023120218/https://zenodo.org/record/1231004 |archive-date=23 October 2018 |access-date=12 June 2019}}</ref> and it results in strong latitudinal [[wind shear]].<ref name="apj125">{{Cite journal |last1=Max |first1=C. E. |last2=Macintosh |first2=B. A. |last3=Gibbard |first3=S. G. |last4=Gavel |first4=D. T. |last5=Roe |first5=H. G. |last6=de Pater |first6=I. |last7=Ghez |first7=A. M. |author-link7=Andrea Ghez |last8=Acton |first8=D. S. |last9=Lai |first9=O. |last10=Stomski |first10=P. |last11=Wizinowich |first11=P. L. |display-authors=4 |date=January 2003 |title=Cloud Structures on Neptune Observed with Keck Telescope Adaptive Optics |journal=[[The Astronomical Journal]] |volume=125 |issue=1 |pages=364–375 |bibcode=2003AJ....125..364M |doi=10.1086/344943 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Magnetosphere ===
Neptune's [[magnetosphere]] consists of a [[magnetic field]] that is strongly tilted relative to its [[Rotation|rotational axis]] at 47° and offset of at least 0.55&nbsp;radius (~13,500&nbsp;km) from the planet's physical centre—resembling Uranus's magnetosphere. Before the arrival of ''Voyager 2'' to Neptune, it was hypothesized that Uranus's sideways rotation caused its tilted magnetosphere. In comparing the magnetic fields of the two planets, scientists now think the extreme orientation may be characteristic of flows in the planets' interiors. This field may be generated by [[convection|convective]] fluid motions in a thin spherical shell of [[Electrical conductor|electrically conducting]] liquids (probably a combination of ammonia, methane and water),<ref name=elkins-tanton>{{cite book |last=Elkins-Tanton |first=Linda T. |date=2006 |title=Uranus, Neptune, Pluto, and the Outer Solar System |publisher=Chelsea House |location=New York |isbn=978-0-8160-5197-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/uranusneptuneplu00elki/page/79 79–83] |url=https://archive.org/details/uranusneptuneplu00elki/page/79 }}</ref> resulting in a [[dynamo]] action.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stanley |first1=Sabine |author-link1=Sabine Stanley |last2=Bloxham |first2=Jeremy |date=March 2004 |title=Convective-region geometry as the cause of Uranus' and Neptune's unusual magnetic fields |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=428 |issue=6979 |pages=151–153 |bibcode=2004Natur.428..151S |doi=10.1038/nature02376 |pmid=15014493 }}</ref>

The dipole component of the magnetic field at the magnetic equator of Neptune is about 14&nbsp;[[Tesla (unit)|microteslas]] (0.14&nbsp;[[Gauss (unit)|G]]).<ref name=Connerney1991>{{cite journal |last1=Connerney |first1=J.E.P. |last2=Acuña |first2=Mario H. |last3=Ness |first3=Norman F. |title=The magnetic field of Neptune |date=1991 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |volume=96 |pages=19,023–42 |bibcode=1991JGR....9619023C |doi=10.1029/91JA01165}}</ref> The dipole [[magnetic moment]] of Neptune is about 2.2{{E-sp|17}}&nbsp;T·m<sup>3</sup> (14&nbsp;μT·''R''<sub>''N''</sub><sup>3</sup>, where ''R''<sub>''N''</sub> is the radius of Neptune). Neptune's magnetic field has a complex geometry that includes relatively large contributions from non-dipolar components, including a strong [[quadrupole]] moment that may exceed the [[Magnetic dipole|dipole]] moment in strength. By contrast, Earth, Jupiter and Saturn have only relatively small quadrupole moments, and their fields are less tilted from the polar axis. The large quadrupole moment of Neptune may be the result of an offset from the planet's centre and geometrical constraints of the field's dynamo generator.<ref name="science4936">{{Cite journal |last1=Ness |first1=Norman F. |last2=Acuña |first2=Mario H. |last3=Burlaga |first3=Leonard F. |last4=Connerney |first4=John E. P. |last5=Lepping |first5=Ronald P. |last6=Neubauer |first6=Fritz M. |date=15 December 1989 |title=Magnetic Fields at Neptune |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1230994 |url-status=live |journal=Science |volume=246 |issue=4936 |pages=1473–1478 |bibcode=1989Sci...246.1473N |doi=10.1126/science.246.4936.1473 |pmid=17756002 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190710235516/https://zenodo.org/record/1230994/files/article.pdf |archive-date=10 July 2019 |access-date=25 August 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hubbard |first1=William B. |title=Encyclopedia of Planetary Science |chapter=Neptune |series=Encyclopedia of Earth Science |date=1997 |pages=521–523 |doi=10.1007/1-4020-4520-4_275 |isbn=0-412-06951-2 }}</ref>

Neptune's [[bow shock]], where the magnetosphere begins to slow the [[solar wind]], occurs at a distance of 34.9 times the radius of the planet. The [[magnetopause]], where the pressure of the magnetosphere counterbalances the solar wind, lies at a distance of 23–26.5 times the radius of Neptune. The tail of the magnetosphere extends out to at least 72 times the radius of Neptune, and likely much farther.<ref name=science4936/>

[[File:Neptune with Aurorae.png|thumb|Left: a visible light image of Neptune taken by the Hubble Space Telescope.{{pb}}Right: the Hubble image composited with a near-infrared image taken by the James Webb Telescope. As the aurorae cannot be observed in the visible band, their image in near-infrared has been rendered as shades of cyan.]]
Measurements by ''Voyager 2'' in extreme-ultraviolet and radio frequencies revealed that Neptune has faint and weak but complex and unique [[aurora]]e; however, these observations were limited in time and did not contain infrared. Subsequent astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope have not glimpsed the aurorae, in contrast to the more well-defined aurorae of Uranus.<ref name="Lamy 2020 p. 20190481">{{cite journal | last=Lamy | first=L. | title=Auroral emissions from Uranus and Neptune | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | publisher=The Royal Society | volume=378 | issue=2187 | date=9 November 2020 | doi=10.1098/rsta.2019.0481 | article-number=20190481| doi-access=free | pmid=33161867 | pmc=7658782 | bibcode=2020RSPTA.37890481L }}</ref><ref name="esa">{{cite web|url=http://www.esa.int/esaCP/SEMLQ71DU8E_index_0.html|title=ESA Portal – Mars Express discovers auroras on Mars|publisher=European Space Agency|date=11 August 2004|access-date=5 August 2010|archive-date=19 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019183824/http://www.esa.int/esaCP/SEMLQ71DU8E_index_0.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2023 the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] observed Neptune's atmosphere and made the first detection of the [[trihydrogen cation]] (<chem>H3+</chem>) at the planet. This finding was only possible due to the increased spatial resolution of JWST which allowed separation of the narrow <chem>H3+</chem> emissions from the broad reflected sunlight of the clouds below. Some of these emissions follow temperature, ion density, and spatial trends consistent with aurora, implying this was also the first observation of Neptune's infrared aurora.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Melin |first1=Henrik |last2=Moore |first2=Luke |last3=Fletcher |first3=Leigh N. |last4=Hammel |first4=Heidi B. |last5=O’Donoghue |first5=James |last6=Stallard |first6=Tom S. |last7=Milam |first7=Stephanie N. |last8=Roman |first8=Michael |last9=King |first9=Oliver R. T. |last10=Rowe-Gurney |first10=Naomi |last11=Thomas |first11=Emma E. |last12=Wang |first12=Ruoyan |last13=Tiranti |first13=Paola I. |last14=Harkett |first14=Jake |last15=Knowles |first15=Katie L. |title=Discovery of H3+ and infrared aurorae at Neptune with JWST |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-025-02507-9 |journal=Nature Astronomy |language=en |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=666–671 |doi=10.1038/s41550-025-02507-9 |issn=2397-3366 |pmc=12095041 |pmid=40417327 |publication-date=2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260527052717/https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-025-02507-9 |archive-date=27 May 2026 |access-date=2 June 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> The nature of Neptune's aurorae is greatly influenced by the peculiar nature of its magnetic field. Both Uranus' and Neptune's magnetic poles are not aligned with the planets' rotational poles, making their aurorae mostly occur around the mid-latitudes rather than the poles like Earth or Jupiter.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ness |first1=Norman |last2=Acuña |first2=Mario H. |last3=Burlaga |first3=Leonard F. |last4=Connerney |first4=John E. P. |last5=Lepping |first5=Ronald P. |last6=Neubauer |first6=Fritz M. |date=1984 |title=Magnetic Fields at Neptune |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.246.4936.1473 |journal=Science |volume=246 |issue=4936 |pages=1473–1478 |doi=10.1126/science.246.4936.1473 |pmid=17756002 |bibcode=1989Sci...246.1473N |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250531080242/https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.246.4936.1473 |archive-date=31 May 2025 |access-date=2 June 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Colour ==
Neptune's atmosphere is faintly blue in the [[Visible spectrum|optical spectrum]], only slightly more saturated than the blue of Uranus's atmosphere.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2024-01-05|title=New images reveal what Neptune and Uranus really look like {{!}} Oxford University|url=https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2024-01-05-new-images-reveal-what-neptune-and-uranus-really-look-0|access-date=2026-05-15|website=www.ox.ac.uk|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240503045100/https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2024-01-05-new-images-reveal-what-neptune-and-uranus-really-look-0|archive-date=3 May 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> This is due to the presence of [[methane]] in its atmosphere.<ref>{{Cite web|title=All About Neptune {{!}} NASA Space Place – NASA Science for Kids|url=https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/all-about-neptune/en/|access-date=2026-05-15|website=spaceplace.nasa.gov|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260610083951/https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/all-about-neptune/en/|archive-date=10 June 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 25 August 1989, the Voyager 2 spacecraft performed a flyby of Neptune; its renderings greatly exaggerated Neptune's colour contrast "to better reveal the clouds, bands and winds", making it seem deep blue compared to Uranus's off-white, creating the myth that Neptune was a deep azure colour.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.space.com/uranus-neptune-similar-shades-of-blue-voyager-2-images|title=Uranus and Neptune are actually similar blues, 'true' color images reveal|author1=Sharmila Kuthunur|date=5 January 2024|website=Space|access-date=8 June 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260522235329/https://www.space.com/uranus-neptune-similar-shades-of-blue-voyager-2-images|archive-date=22 May 2026|url-status=live}}</ref> The two planets had been imaged with different systems, making it hard to directly compare the resulting [[Compositing|composite images]]. This was revisited with the colour normalized over time, most comprehensively in late 2023.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=Irwin/>

<gallery widths="200" heights="200" class="center">
File:Neptune Full.jpg|Original 2-colour (orange-green) NASA/JPL image from [[Voyager 2|''Voyager&nbsp;2'']], with exaggerated colour<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catalog Page for PIA01492 |url=https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA01492 |access-date=2024-02-05 |website=photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov |date=30 October 1998 |archive-date=22 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230722014419/https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA01492 |url-status=live }}</ref>
File:Neptune - Voyager 2 (29347980845) flatten crop.jpg|Colour recalibrated in 2016 (Justin Cowart), preserving some enhancement for contrast<ref>{{Cite web |title=The subtle color difference between Uranus and Neptune |url=https://www.planetary.org/articles/uranus-neptune-color-difference |access-date=2024-02-05 |website=The Planetary Society |archive-date=5 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240205080048/https://www.planetary.org/articles/uranus-neptune-color-difference |url-status=live }}</ref>

</gallery>

== Atmosphere ==
{{Multiple image
| direction   = vertical
| total_width = 230
| image1      = Neptune Cloud Cover Over Three Decades (2023-019).png
| caption1    = Neptune's cloud cover from 1994 to 2020.<ref name="NYT-20230818" /> False colour image based on data from [[WFPC2]] and [[WFC3]] instruments of the [[Hubble Space Telescope]].
| image2      = Neptune clouds.jpg
| caption2    = Bands of high-altitude clouds cast shadows on Neptune's lower cloud deck. The colour is exaggerated to show the clouds more clearly.
}}

At high altitudes, Neptune's atmosphere is 80% [[hydrogen]] and 19% [[helium]].<ref name=hubbard>{{cite journal |last=Hubbard |first=W.B. |title=Neptune's Deep Chemistry |journal=Science |date=1997 |volume=275 |issue=5304 |pages=1279–80 |doi=10.1126/science.275.5304.1279 |pmid=9064785 }}</ref> A trace amount of [[methane]] is present. Prominent absorption bands of methane exist at wavelengths above 600&nbsp;nm, in the red and infrared portion of the spectrum. As with Uranus, this absorption of red light by atmospheric methane is part of what gives Neptune its faint blue hue,<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Crisp |first1=D. |last2=Hammel |first2=H.B. |date=14 June 1995 |title=Hubble Space Telescope Observations of Neptune |url=http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/1995/09/image/a/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070802132430/http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/1995/09/image/a |archive-date=2 August 2007 |access-date=22 April 2007 |publisher=Hubble News Center}}</ref> which is more pronounced for Neptune due to concentrated haze in Uranus's atmosphere.<ref name="NYT-20240104">{{cite news |last=Ferreira |first=Becky |title=Uranus and Neptune Reveal Their True Colors - Neptune is not as blue as you've been led to believe, and Uranus's shifting colors are better explained, in new research. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/01/04/science/uranus-neptune-colors-blue.html |date=4 January 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240105114302/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/01/04/science/uranus-neptune-colors-blue.html |archive-date= 2024-01-05|access-date=5 January 2024 }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web
 | author=NASA Science Editorial Team
 | title=Why Uranus and Neptune Are Different Colors
 | date=31 May 2022
 | publisher=NASA
 | url=https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/neptune/why-uranus-and-neptune-are-different-colors/
 | access-date=30 October 2023
 | archive-date=31 October 2023
 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031014930/https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/neptune/why-uranus-and-neptune-are-different-colors/
 | url-status=live
 }}</ref>

Neptune's atmosphere is subdivided into two main regions: the lower [[troposphere]], where temperature decreases with altitude, and the [[stratosphere]], where temperature increases with altitude. The boundary between the two, the [[tropopause]], lies at a pressure of {{convert|0.1|bar|kPa}}.<ref name="Lunine 1993"/> The stratosphere then gives way to the [[thermosphere]] at a pressure lower than 10<sup>−5</sup> to 10<sup>−4</sup>&nbsp;bars (1 to 10&nbsp;Pa).<ref name="Lunine 1993"/> The thermosphere gradually transitions to the [[exosphere]].<ref name="l086">{{cite web | last=Williams | first=Matt | title=The gas (and ice) giant Neptune | website=Phys.org | date=14 September 2015 | url=https://phys.org/news/2015-09-gas-ice-giant-neptune.html | access-date=27 August 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240912090857/https://phys.org/news/2015-09-gas-ice-giant-neptune.html | archive-date=12 September 2024 | url-status=live}}</ref>

Models suggest that Neptune's troposphere is banded by clouds of varying compositions depending on altitude.<ref name="NYT-20230818">{{cite news |last=Andrews |first=Robin George |title=Neptune's Clouds Have Vanished, and Scientists Think They Know Why - A recent study suggests a relationship between solar cycles and the atmosphere of the solar system's eighth planet. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/18/science/neptune-clouds-sun.html |date=18 August 2023 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230821110635/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/18/science/neptune-clouds-sun.html |archive-date= 2023-08-21|access-date=21 August 2023 }}</ref> The upper-level clouds lie at pressures below one bar, where the temperature is suitable for methane to condense. For pressures between one and five bars (100 and 500&nbsp;kPa), clouds of [[ammonia]] and [[hydrogen sulfide]] are thought to form. Above a pressure of five bars, the clouds may consist of ammonia, [[ammonium sulfide]], hydrogen sulfide and water. Deeper clouds of water ice should be found at pressures of about {{convert|50|bar|MPa}}, where the temperature reaches {{Convert|273|K|C F}}. Underneath, clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide may be found.<ref name=elkins-tanton/>

High-altitude clouds on Neptune have been observed casting shadows on the opaque cloud deck below. There are high-altitude cloud bands that wrap around the planet at constant latitudes. These circumferential bands have widths of 50–150&nbsp;km and lie about 50–110&nbsp;km above the cloud deck.<ref name=apj125/> These altitudes are in the layer where weather occurs, the troposphere. Weather does not occur in the higher stratosphere or thermosphere. In August 2023, the high-altitude clouds of Neptune vanished, prompting reference to a study spanning thirty years of observations by the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based telescopes. The study found that Neptune's high-altitude cloud activity is bound to [[Solar cycle]]s, and not to the planet's seasons.<ref name="NYT-20230818" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Gianopoulos |first1=Andrea |title=Neptune's Disappearing Clouds Linked to the Solar Cycle |url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/2023/hubble-neptunes-disappearing-clouds-linked-to-the-solar-cycle |website=NASA |access-date=24 August 2023 |date=16 August 2023 |archive-date=24 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230824000143/https://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/2023/hubble-neptunes-disappearing-clouds-linked-to-the-solar-cycle/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chavez |first1=Erandi |last2=de Pater |first2=Imke |last3=Redwing |first3=Erin |last4=Molter |first4=Edward M. |last5=Roman |first5=Michael T. |last6=Zorzi |first6=Andrea |last7=Alvarez |first7=Carlos |last8=Campbell |first8=Randy |last9=de Kleer |first9=Katherine|author9-link=Katherine de Kleer |last10=Hueso |first10=Ricardo |last11=Wong |first11=Michael H. |last12=Gates |first12=Elinor |last13=Lynam |first13=Paul David |last14=Davies |first14=Ashley G. |last15=Aycock |first15=Joel |last16=Mcilroy |first16=Jason |last17=Pelletier |first17=John |last18=Ridenour |first18=Anthony |last19=Stickel |first19=Terry |title=Evolution of Neptune at near-infrared wavelengths from 1994 through 2022 |journal=Icarus |date=November 2023 |volume=404 |article-number=115667 |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2023.115667 |arxiv=2307.08157 |bibcode=2023Icar..40415667C |quote=The clear positive correlation we find between cloud activity and Solar Lyman-Alpha (121.56 nm) irradiance lends support to the theory that the periodicity in Neptune's cloud activity results from photochemical cloud/haze production triggered by Solar ultraviolet emissions. }}</ref>

Neptune's [[Visible spectrum|spectra]] suggest that its lower stratosphere is hazy due to condensation of products of ultraviolet [[photolysis]] of methane, such as [[ethane]] and [[acetylene|ethyne]].<ref name="Lunine 1993"/><ref name=hubbard/> The stratosphere is home to trace amounts of [[carbon monoxide]] and [[hydrogen cyanide]].<ref name="Lunine 1993"/><ref name="Encrenaz 2003"/> The stratosphere of Neptune is warmer than that of Uranus due to the elevated concentration of hydrocarbons.<ref name="Lunine 1993"/>

For reasons that remain obscure, the planet's thermosphere is at an anomalously high temperature of about {{Convert|750|K|C F|sigfig=3}}.<ref name="Broadfoot19989">{{cite journal |last1=Broadfoot |first1=A. L. |last2=Atreya |first2=S. K. |last3=Bertaux |first3=J. L. |last4=Blamont |first4=J. E. |last5=Dessler |first5=A. J. |last6=Donahue |first6=T. M. |last7=Forrester |first7=W. T. |last8=Hall |first8=D. T. |last9=Herbert |first9=F. |last10=Holberg |first10=J. B. |last11=Hunter |first11=D. M. |last12=Krasnopolsky |first12=V. A. |last13=Linick |first13=S. |last14=Lunine |first14=J. I. |last15=McConnell |first15=J. C. |author16-link=Henry Warren Moos |last16=Moos |first16=H. W. |last17=Sandel |first17=B. R. |last18=Schneider |first18=N. M. |last19=Shemansky |first19=D. E. |last20=Smith |first20=G. R. |last21=Strobel |first21=D. F. |last22=Yelle |first22=R. V. |title=Ultraviolet Spectrometer Observations of Neptune and Triton |journal=Science |date=15 December 1989 |volume=246 |issue=4936 |pages=1459–1466 |doi=10.1126/science.246.4936.1459 |pmid=17756000 |bibcode=1989Sci...246.1459B }}</ref><ref name="Herbert & Sandel 1999"/> The planet is too far from the Sun for this heat to be generated by [[ultraviolet]] radiation. One candidate for a heating mechanism is atmospheric interaction with ions in the planet's [[Magnetosphere|magnetic field]]. Other candidates are [[gravity wave]]s from the interior that dissipate in the atmosphere. The first observation of <chem>H3+</chem> in Neptune's [[ionosphere]], co-located with the thermosphere, also lead to the first temperature measurement of Neptune's thermosphere since ''Voyager 2'' of 450 K; thus, Neptune is experiencing an unexplained, extreme cooling trend of ~10 K per year.<ref name=":2" /> This cooling trend is also occurring in Uranus' upper atmosphere and is much better documented.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Melin |first1=Henrik |last2=Fletcher |first2=L. N. |last3=Hammel |first3=H. B. |last4=Milam |first4=S. N. |last5=Moore |first5=L. |last6=Stallard |first6=T. S. |last7=O’Donoghue |first7=J. |last8=Tiranti |first8=P. I. |last9=Thomas |first9=E. M. |last10=Knowles |first10=K. L. |last11=Roman |first11=M. |last12=Lamy |first12=L. |last13=King |first13=O. R. T. |last14=Harkett |first14=J. |date=2025-11-28 |title=The Ionosphere of Uranus as Revealed by JWST |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2025GL118301 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |language=en |volume=52 |issue=22 |article-number=e2025GL118301 |doi=10.1029/2025GL118301 |bibcode=2025GeoRL..5218301M |issn=0094-8276|doi-access=free }}</ref> The thermosphere contains traces of [[carbon dioxide]] and water, which may have been deposited from external sources such as [[meteorite]]s and dust.<ref name=elkins-tanton/><ref name="Encrenaz 2003"/> 

=== Climate ===
[[File:Neptune storms.jpg|thumb|The [[Great Dark Spot]] (top), Scooter (middle white cloud),<ref name=scooter>{{cite web |first=Sue |last=Lavoie |date=8 January 1998 |title=PIA01142: Neptune Scooter |url=http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA01142 |publisher=NASA |access-date=26 March 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029200323/http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA01142 |archive-date=29 October 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> and the [[Small Dark Spot]] (bottom), with contrast exaggerated]]

Neptune's weather is characterized by extremely dynamic storm systems, with winds reaching speeds of almost {{cvt|600|m/s|km/h mph}}—exceeding [[supersonic speed|supersonic]] flow.<ref name="Suomi1991" /> More typically, by tracking the motion of persistent clouds, wind speeds have been shown to vary from 20&nbsp;m/s in the easterly direction to 325&nbsp;m/s westward.<ref name="Hammel1989">{{cite journal |last1=Hammel |first1=H. B. |last2=Beebe |first2=R. F. |last3=De Jong |first3=E. M. |last4=Hansen |first4=C. J. |last5=Howell |first5=C. D. |last6=Ingersoll |first6=A. P. |last7=Johnson |first7=T. V. |last8=Limaye |first8=S. S. |last9=Magalhães |first9=J. A. |last10=Pollack |first10=J. B. |last11=Sromovsky |first11=L. A. |last12=Suomi |first12=V. E. |last13=Swift |first13=C. E. |title=Neptune's Wind Speeds Obtained by Tracking Clouds in Voyager Images |journal=Science |date=22 September 1989 |volume=245 |issue=4924 |pages=1367–1369 |doi=10.1126/science.245.4924.1367 |pmid=17798743 |bibcode=1989Sci...245.1367H }}</ref> At the cloud tops, the prevailing winds range in speed from 400&nbsp;m/s along the equator to 250&nbsp;m/s at the poles.<ref name=elkins-tanton/> Most of the winds on Neptune move in a direction opposite the planet's rotation.<ref name=burgess2>[[#Burgess|Burgess]] (1991):64–70.</ref> The general pattern of winds showed prograde rotation at high latitudes vs. retrograde rotation at lower latitudes. The difference in flow direction is thought to be a "[[skin effect]]" and not due to any deeper atmospheric processes.<ref name="Lunine 1993"/> At 70°S latitude, a high-speed jet travels at a speed of 300&nbsp;m/s.<ref name="Lunine 1993"/> Due to seasonal changes, the cloud bands in the southern hemisphere of Neptune have been observed to increase in size and [[albedo]]. This trend was first seen in 1980. The long orbital period of Neptune results in seasons lasting 40 Earth years.<ref name="villard">{{Cite news |last1=Villard |first1=Ray |last2=Devitt |first2=Terry |date=15 May 2003 |title=Brighter Neptune Suggests A Planetary Change of Seasons |url=http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/2003/17/text/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080228081218/http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/2003/17/text/ |archive-date=28 February 2008 |access-date=26 February 2008 |publisher=Hubble News Center}}</ref>

Neptune differs from Uranus in its typical level of [[Meteorology|meteorological]] activity. ''Voyager 2'' observed weather phenomena on Neptune during its 1989 flyby,<ref name=spot/> but no comparable phenomena on Uranus during its 1986 flyby.

The abundance of methane, ethane and [[acetylene]] at Neptune's equator is 10–100 times greater than at the poles. This is interpreted as evidence for [[upwelling]] at the equator and subsidence near the poles, as photochemistry cannot account for the distribution without meridional circulation.<ref name="Lunine 1993"/>

In 2007, it was discovered that the upper troposphere of Neptune's south pole was about 10 K warmer than the rest of its atmosphere, which averages about {{Convert|73|K|C|round=5}}. The temperature differential is enough to let methane, which elsewhere is frozen in the troposphere, escape into the stratosphere near the pole.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Orton |first1=G. S. |last2=Encrenaz |first2=T. |author-link2=Thérèse Encrenaz |last3=Leyrat |first3=C. |last4=Puetter |first4=R. |last5=Friedson |first5=A. J. |display-authors=4 |name-list-style=amp |date=October 2007 |title=Evidence for methane escape and strong seasonal and dynamical perturbations of Neptune's atmospheric temperatures |journal=[[Astronomy & Astrophysics]] |volume=473 |issue=1 |pages=L5–L8 |bibcode=2007A&A...473L...5O |doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20078277 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The relative "hot spot" is due to Neptune's [[axial tilt]], which has exposed the south pole to the [[Sun]] for the last quarter of Neptune's year, or roughly 40 Earth years. As Neptune slowly moves towards the opposite side of the Sun, the south pole will be darkened and the north pole illuminated, causing the methane release to shift to the north pole.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Orton |first1=Glenn |last2=Encrenaz |first2=Thérèse |author-link2=Thérèse Encrenaz |date=18 September 2007 |title=A Warm South Pole? Yes, On Neptune! |url=http://www.eso.org/public/news/eso0741/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100323211637/http://www.eso.org/public/news/eso0741/ |archive-date=23 March 2010 |access-date=20 September 2007 |publisher=[[ESO]]}}</ref>

==== Storms ====
[[File:Neptune's Great Dark Spot colorcorrected.jpg|thumb|255x255px|The Great Dark Spot imaged by ''Voyager 2'']]
In 1989, the [[Great Dark Spot]], an [[anticyclone|anticyclonic]] storm system spanning {{convert|13000 x 6,600|km|mi|abbr=on}},<ref name=spot>{{cite web |last=Lavoie |first=Sue |date=16 February 2000 |url=http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA02245 |title=PIA02245: Neptune's blue-green atmosphere |publisher=NASA JPL |access-date=28 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130805215059/http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA02245 |archive-date=5 August 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> was discovered by [[NASA]]'s ''Voyager 2'' spacecraft. The storm resembled the [[Great Red Spot]] of Jupiter. Some five years later, on 2 November 1994, the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] did not see the Great Dark Spot on the planet. Instead, a new storm similar to the Great Dark Spot was found in Neptune's northern hemisphere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hammel |first1=H. B. |last2=Lockwood | first2=G. W. | last3=Mills | first3=J. R. | last4=Barnet | first4=C. D. |title=Hubble Space Telescope Imaging of Neptune's Cloud Structure in 1994 |journal=Science |date=1995 |volume=268 |issue=5218 |pages=1740–42 |doi=10.1126/science.268.5218.1740 |pmid=17834994 |bibcode=1995Sci...268.1740H }}</ref>

The {{vanchor|Scooter}} is another storm, a white cloud group farther south than the Great Dark Spot. This nickname first arose during the months leading up to the ''Voyager 2'' encounter in 1989, when they were observed moving at speeds faster than the Great Dark Spot (and images acquired later would subsequently reveal the presence of clouds moving even faster than those that had initially been detected by ''Voyager 2'').<ref name="burgess2" /> The [[Small Dark Spot]] is a southern cyclonic storm, the second-most-intense storm observed during the 1989 encounter. It was initially completely dark, but as ''Voyager 2'' approached the planet, a bright core developed, which can be seen in most of the highest-resolution images.<ref>{{cite web |last=Lavoie |first=Sue |date=29 January 1996 |url=http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA00064 |title=PIA00064: Neptune's Dark Spot (D2) at High Resolution |publisher=NASA JPL |access-date=28 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927090039/http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA00064 |archive-date=27 September 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2018, a newer main dark spot and smaller dark spot were identified and studied.<ref name="NYT-20201222">{{Cite news |last=Stirone |first=Shannon |author-link=Shannon Stirone |date=22 December 2020 |title=Neptune's Weird Dark Spot Just Got Weirder – While observing the planet's large inky storm, astronomers spotted a smaller vortex they named Dark Spot Jr. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/22/science/neptune-dark-spot.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222101200/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/22/science/neptune-dark-spot.html |archive-date=22 December 2020 |access-date=22 December 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> In 2023, the first ground-based observation of a dark spot on Neptune was announced.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mysterious Neptune dark spot detected from Earth for the first time |url=https://www.eso.org/public/news/eso2314/ |access-date=26 August 2023 |publisher=[[ESO]] |archive-date=26 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230826075848/https://www.eso.org/public/news/eso2314/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
