A '''black hole''' is an [[astronomical body]] so [[compact object|compact]] that its [[gravity]] prevents anything, including [[light]], from escaping. [[Albert Einstein]]'s theory of [[general relativity]], which describes gravitation as the [[curvature of spacetime]], predicts that any sufficiently compact [[mass]] will form a black hole.<ref name="NYT-20150608">{{Cite news |last=Overbye |first=Dennis | author-link=Dennis Overbye |date=8 June 2015 |title=Black Hole Hunters |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/06/09/science/black-hole-event-horizon-telescope.html |access-date=28 March 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150609023631/http://www.nytimes.com/2015/06/09/science/black-hole-event-horizon-telescope.html |archive-date=9 June 2015}}</ref> The [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of no escape is called the [[event horizon]]. In general relativity, crossing a black hole's event horizon traps an object inside but produces no locally detectable change. General relativity also predicts that every black hole should have a central [[gravitational singularity|singularity]], where the curvature of spacetime is infinite.

Objects whose [[gravitational field]]s are too strong for light to escape were first considered in the 18th century. In 1916, the first solution of general relativity that would characterise a black hole was found. By the late 1950s, this solution began to be interpreted physically as a region of space from which nothing can escape. Black holes were long considered a mathematical curiosity; it was not until the 1960s that theoretical work showed they were a generic prediction of general relativity. The first widely accepted black hole was [[Cygnus X-1]], an [[astrophysical X-ray source|x-ray source]]  proposed as a black hole binary through several studies between 1971 and 1974.

Black holes typically form as part of a [[supernova]] event when massive stars collapse at the end of their [[stellar evolution|life cycle]]. After a black hole has formed, it can grow by absorbing mass from its surroundings. Supermassive black holes of millions of [[solar mass]]es may form by absorbing stars and merging with other black holes, or via [[Direct collapse black hole|direct collapse]] of [[gas cloud]]s. There is consensus that [[supermassive black hole]]s exist in the centres of most [[galaxies]].

[[Quantum field theory in curved spacetime]] predicts that event horizons emit [[Hawking radiation]], with the rate of emission being inversely proportional to the mass. This causes the black hole to lose mass very slowly, provided it is not [[accretion (astrophysics)|accreting]] matter. However, even the smallest class of black holes observed, [[stellar black hole]]s, are gaining mass from the [[cosmic microwave background]] faster than they are losing mass via Hawking radiation.

The presence of a black hole can be inferred through its interaction with [[matter]] and [[electromagnetic radiation]] such as visible light. Matter falling toward a black hole can form an [[accretion disk]] of infalling plasma, heated by [[friction]] and emitting light. In extreme cases, this creates a [[quasar]], some of the brightest objects in the universe. Merging black holes can be [[interferometry|detected]] by the [[gravitational wave]]s they emit. If stars are orbiting a black hole, their motions can be used to determine the black hole's mass and location. In this way, astronomers have identified numerous stellar black hole candidates in [[binary star|binary systems]] and established that the radio source known as [[Sagittarius A*]], at the core of the [[Milky Way]] galaxy, contains a supermassive black hole of about 4.3{{nbsp}}million solar masses.

{{toclimit|4}}

== History ==
{{Main|History of black hole physics}}

The idea of a body so massive that even light could not escape was first proposed in the late 18th century by English astronomer and clergyman [[John Michell]] and independently by French scientist [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]]. Both scholars proposed very large stars in contrast to the modern concept of an extremely dense object.<ref name="origin">{{cite journal |last1=Montgomery |first1=Colin |last2=Orchiston |first2=Wayne |last3=Whittingham |first3=Ian |title=Michell, Laplace and the Origin of the Black Hole Concept |journal=[[Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage]] |date=2009 |type=Research article |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=90–96 |bibcode=2009JAHH...12...90M |doi=10.3724/SP.J.1440-2807.2009.02.01 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Michell's idea, in a short part of a letter published in 1784,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Michell |first=J. |author-link1=John Michell |date=1784 |title=On the Means of Discovering the Distance, Magnitude, &C. Of the Fixed Stars, In Consequence of the Diminution of the Velocity of Their Light, In Case Such a Diminution Should Be Found to Take Place in Any of Them, And Such Other Data Should Be Procured from Observations, As Would Be Farther Necessary for That Purpose |journal=[[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society]] | volume=74 |pages=35–57 |bibcode=1784RSPT...74...35M |doi=10.1098/rstl.1784.0008 |jstor=106576 |doi-access=free}}</ref> calculated that a star with the same density but 500 times the radius of the [[Sun]] would not let any emitted light escape; the surface [[escape velocity]] would exceed the [[speed of light]].<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|122}} Michell correctly hypothesized that such non-radiating bodies might be detectable through their gravitational effects on nearby visible bodies. In 1796, while speculating on the [[origin of the Solar System]] in his book {{lang|fr|Exposition du Système du Monde}}, Laplace made a qualitative suggestion that a star could be invisible if it were sufficiently large. [[Franz Xaver von Zach]] asked Laplace for a mathematical analysis, which Laplace provided and published in von Zach's journal ''{{Interlanguage link|Allgemeine Geographische Ephemeriden|de}}''.<ref name="origin" />

=== General relativity ===
{{See also|History of general relativity}}
{{General relativity sidebar|phenomena}}

In 1905, [[Albert Einstein]] showed that the laws of [[electromagnetism]] are identical for observers travelling at different velocities relative to each other. The laws of [[mechanics]] had already been shown to be invariant in this way. However, the theory of gravitation was yet to be included.<ref name="Weinberg-1972">{{cite book |last=Weinberg |first=Steven |url=https://archive.org/details/gravitationcosmo00stev_0 |title=Gravitation and Cosmology |date=1972 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-471-92567-5 |author-link=Steven Weinberg |url-access=registration}}</ref>{{rp|19}}

In 1907, Einstein published a paper proposing his [[equivalence principle]], the hypothesis that [[inertial mass]] and [[gravitational mass]] have a common cause. Using the principle, Einstein predicted the [[redshift]] and the [[gravitational lensing|lensing]] effect of gravity on light; his prediction of gravitational lensing was one-half of the value that the full theory of general relativity would predict.<ref name="Weinberg-1972" />{{rp|19}} By 1915, Einstein refined these ideas into his [[general theory of relativity]], which explained how matter affects spacetime, which in turn affects the motion of other matter.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Einstein |first1=Albert |author-link=Albert Einstein |date=1915 |title=Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation |trans-title=Field Equations of Gravitation |language=de |pages=844–847 |journal=Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften |bibcode=1915SPAW.......844E |bibcode-access=free |hdl=2027/umn.31951d000117420?urlappend=%3Bseq=376%3Bownerid=13510798903261489-394 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Janssen |first1=Michel |last2=Renn |first2=Jürgen |author-link2=Jürgen Renn |date=2015 |title=Arch and Scaffold: How Einstein Found His Field Equations |journal=[[Physics Today]] | type=Feature article |volume=68 |issue=11 |pages=30–36 |bibcode=2015PhT....68k..30J |doi=10.1063/PT.3.2979 |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-002A-8ED7-1 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free}}</ref> This formed the basis for black hole [[astrophysics]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Fraknoi |first1=Andrew |author-link1=Andrew Fraknoi |url=https://assets.openstax.org/oscms-prodcms/media/documents/Astronomy2e-WEB.pdf |title=Astronomy 2e |last2=Morrison |first2=David |author-link2=David Morrison (astrophysicist) |last3=Wolff |first3=Sidney C. |author-link3=Sidney C. Wolff |date=2022 |publisher=[[OpenStax]] |isbn=978-1-951693-50-3 |edition=2e |pages=839–846 |chapter=24.5 Black Holes |oclc=1322188620 |display-authors= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250725091512/https://assets.openstax.org/oscms-prodcms/media/documents/Astronomy2e-WEB.pdf|archive-date=25 Jul 2025}}</ref>

=== Singular solutions in general relativity ===
Only a few months after Einstein published the [[Einstein field equations|field equations]] describing general relativity, astrophysicist [[Karl Schwarzschild]] set out to apply the idea to stars. He assumed spherical symmetry with no [[stellar rotation|spin]] and found a [[Schwarzschild metric|solution]] to Einstein's equations.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|124}}<ref name="Schwarzschild1916">{{cite journal |last=Schwarzschild |first=K. |author-link1=Karl Schwarzschild |date=1916 |title=Über das Gravitationsfeld eines Massenpunktes nach der Einsteinschen Theorie |trans-title=On the gravitational field of a mass point according to Einstein's theory<!-- via translate.google --> |url=https://archive.org/stream/sitzungsberichte1916deutsch#page/188/mode/2up |journal=Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften |volume=7 |pages=189–196 |bibcode=1916SPAW.......189S |via=Internet Archive}}
* Translation: {{cite arXiv |eprint=physics/9905030 |first1=S. |last1=Antoci |first2=A. |last2=Loinger |title=On the Gravitational Field of a Mass Point According to Einstein's Theory |date=12 May 1999<!-- date submitted --> }} and {{cite journal |last=Schwarzschild |first=K. |author-link1=Karl Schwarzschild |date=1916 |title=Über das Gravitationsfeld einer Kugel aus inkompressibler Flüssigkeit nach der Einsteinschen Theorie |url=https://archive.org/stream/sitzungsberichte1916deutsch#page/424/mode/2up |journal=Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften |volume=18 |pages=424–434 |bibcode=1916skpa.conf..424S}}
* Translation: {{cite arXiv |eprint=physics/9912033 |first1=S. |last1=Antoci |title=On the Gravitational Field of a Sphere of Incompressible Fluid According to Einstein's Theory |year=1999 }}</ref> A few months after Schwarzschild, [[Johannes Droste]], a student of [[Hendrik Lorentz]], independently gave the same solution.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Droste |first=J. |date=1917 |title=The Field of a Single Centre in Einstein's Theory of Gravitation, And the Motion of a Particle in That Field |url=http://www.dwc.knaw.nl/DL/publications/PU00012325.pdf |url-status=live |department=Physics |journal=Proceedings of the Section of Sciences |publisher=[[Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen]] | volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=197–215 |bibcode=1917KNAB...19..197D |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130518034708/http://www.dwc.knaw.nl/DL/publications/PU00012325.pdf |archive-date=18 May 2013 |access-date=16 September 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Studies in the History of General Relativity |editor1-last=Eisenstaedt |editor1-first=Jean |editor2-last=Kox |editor2-first=A. J. |isbn=978-0-8176-3479-7 |date=1992 |publisher=Birkhäuser |chapter=General Relativity in the Netherlands: 1915–1920 |last=Kox |first=A. J. |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vDHCF_3vIhUC&pg=PA41 |page=41 |access-date=23 February 2016 |archive-date=10 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160810215219/https://books.google.com/books?id=vDHCF_3vIhUC&pg=PA41 |url-status=live }}</ref> At a certain radius from the centre of the mass, the Schwarzschild solution became [[singularity (mathematics)|singular]], meaning that some of the terms in the Einstein equations became infinite. The nature of this radius, which later became known as the [[Schwarzschild radius]], was not understood at the time.<ref name="HooftHist">{{cite web |last='t Hooft |first=G. |author-link1=Gerard 't Hooft |date=2009 |title=Introduction to the Theory of Black Holes |url=http://www.phys.uu.nl/~thooft/lectures/blackholes/BH_lecturenotes.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090521082736/http://www.phys.uu.nl/~thooft/lectures/blackholes/BH_lecturenotes.pdf |archive-date=21 May 2009 |access-date=24 June 2010 |publisher=Institute for Theoretical Physics / Spinoza Institute |pages=47–48}}</ref>

Many physicists of the early 20th century were sceptical of the existence of black holes. In a 1926 popular science book, [[Arthur Eddington]] critiqued the idea of a star with mass compressed to its Schwarzschild radius as a flaw in the then-poorly-understood theory of general relativity.<ref name="eddington1926">{{cite book |first=Arthur |last=Eddington |author-link=Arthur Eddington |date=1926 |title=The Internal Constitution of the Stars |series=Science |volume=52 |pages=233–40 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RjC9DpnWFbkC&pg=PA6 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160811034409/https://books.google.com/books?id=RjC9DpnWFbkC&lpg=PP1&pg=PA6 |archive-date=11 August 2016 |pmid=17747682 |doi=10.1126/science.52.1341.233|bibcode=1920Sci....52..233E }} {{isbn|978-0-521-33708-3}}</ref><ref name="Thorne-1994">{{cite book |last1=Thorne |first1=Kip S. |author-link=Kip Thorne |url=https://archive.org/details/blackholestimewa0000thor |title=Black Holes and Time Warps: Einstein's Outrageous Legacy |last2=Hawking |first2=Stephen |author-link2=Stephen Hawking |date=1994 |publisher=[[W. W. Norton & Company]] | isbn=978-0-393-31276-8 |editor-last=Agrawal |editor-first=Milan |edition=1st |access-date=12 April 2019 |url-access=registration}}</ref>{{rp|134|q=The first conclusion was the Newtonian version of light not escaping; the second was a semi-accurate, relativistic description; and the third was typical Eddingtonian hyperbole{{nbsp}}[...] when a star is as small as the critical circumference, the curvature is strong but not infinite, and space is definitely not wrapped around the star. Eddington may have known this, but his description made a good story, and it captured in a whimsical way the spirit of Schwarzschild's spacetime curvature.}} In 1939, Einstein used his theory of general relativity in an attempt to prove that black holes were impossible.<ref name="Bernstein-2007">{{cite magazine |last=Bernstein |first=Jeremy |author-link=Jeremy Bernstein |date=2007 |title=The Reluctant Father of Black Holes |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-reluctant-father-of-black-holes-2007-04/ |url-access=subscription |access-date=3 August 2023 |magazine=[[Scientific American]] |pages=4–11 |language=en |volume=17 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0407-4sp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180826111000/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-reluctant-father-of-black-holes-2007-04/ |archive-date=26 August 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Einstein |first=Albert |author-link=Albert Einstein |date=10 May 1939 |title=On a Stationary System With Spherical Symmetry Consisting of Many Gravitating Masses |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] | volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=922–936 |doi=10.2307/1968902 |jstor=1968902 }}</ref> His work relied on increasing pressure or increasing [[centrifugal force]] balancing the force of gravity so that the object would not collapse beyond its Schwarzschild radius. He missed the possibility that implosion would drive the system below this critical value.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|135}}

=== Gravity vs. degeneracy pressure ===
By the 1920s, astronomers had classified a number of [[white dwarf]] stars as too cool and dense to be explained by the gradual cooling of ordinary stars. In 1926, [[Ralph Fowler]] showed that these stars are not like [[main-sequence star]]s, where thermal pressure balances gravity. Instead, a type of [[degeneracy pressure|quantum-mechanical pressure]] balances gravity at these temperatures and densities.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|145}} In 1931, [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] studied the new [[state of matter]] that results from this balance, called [[electron-degenerate matter]], discovering that it is stable below a certain [[Chandrasekhar limit|limiting mass]]. By 1934 he showed that this explained the catalogue of white dwarf stars.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|151}} When Chandrasekhar announced his results, Eddington pointed out that stars above this limit would radiate until they were sufficiently dense to prevent light from exiting, a conclusion he considered absurd. Eddington and, later, [[Lev Landau]] argued that some yet unknown mechanism would stop the collapse.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Detweiler |first=S. |author-link=Steven Detweiler |date=1981 |title=Resource Letter BH-1: Black Holes |journal=[[American Journal of Physics]] | type=Paper |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=394–400 |bibcode=1981AmJPh..49..394D |doi=10.1119/1.12686}}</ref>

In the 1930s, [[Fritz Zwicky]] and [[Walter Baade]] studied [[stellar nova]]e, focusing on exceptionally bright ones they called [[supernova]]e. Zwicky promoted the idea that supernovae produced stars with the density of atomic nuclei—[[neutron star]]s—but this idea was largely ignored at the time.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|171}} In 1939, based on Chandrasekhar's reasoning, but working within general relativity rather than Newtonian gravity, [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] and [[George Volkoff]] predicted that neutron stars below a certain mass limit, later called the [[Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit]], would be stable due to [[neutron degeneracy pressure]].<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|193}} Above that limit, they reasoned that either their model would not apply or that gravitational contraction would not stop.<ref name="OV1939">{{cite journal |last1=Oppenheimer |first1=J. R. |author-link1=J. Robert Oppenheimer |last2=Volkoff |first2=G. M. |author-link2=George Volkoff |date=1939 |title=On Massive Neutron Cores |journal=[[Physical Review]] | volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=374–381 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.55.374|bibcode=1939PhRv...55..374O}}</ref>{{rp |page=380 |quote=There would then seem to be only two answers possible to the question of the behaviour of very massive stars: either the equation of state we have used so far fails to describe the behaviour of highly condensed matter that the conclusions reached above are qualitatively misleading, or the star will continue to contract indefinitely, never reaching equilibrium.}}

[[John Archibald Wheeler]] and two of his students resolved questions about the model behind the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff (TOV) limit. In 1965, Harrison and Wheeler developed the [[equations of state]] relating density to pressure for cold matter all the way through electron degeneracy and neutron degeneracy. Masami Wakano and Wheeler then used the equations to compute the equilibrium curve for stars, relating mass to circumference. They found no additional features that would invalidate the TOV limit. This meant that the only thing that could prevent black holes from forming was a dynamic process ejecting sufficient mass from a star as it cooled.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|205}}

=== Birth of modern model ===
The modern concept of black holes was formulated by [[Robert Oppenheimer]] and his student [[Hartland Snyder]] in 1939.<ref name="Bernstein-2007" /><ref name="Bartusiak" />{{rp|80}} In the paper,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oppenheimer |first1=J.R. |author-link=J. Robert Oppenheimer |last2=Snyder |first2=H. |author-link2=Hartland Snyder |year=1939 |title=On Continued Gravitational Contraction |journal=[[Physical Review]] | type=Highlighted article |volume=56 |issue=5 |pages=455–459 |bibcode=1939PhRv...56..455O |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.56.455 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Oppenheimer and Snyder solved Einstein's equations of general relativity for an idealised imploding star, in a model later called the [[Oppenheimer–Snyder model]], then described the results from far outside the star. The implosion starts as one might expect: the star material rapidly collapses inward. However, as the density of the star increases, [[gravitational time dilation]] increases and the collapse, viewed from afar, seems to slow down further and further until the star reaches its Schwarzschild radius, where it appears frozen in time.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|217}}

In 1958, [[David Finkelstein]] identified the Schwarzschild surface as an [[event horizon]], calling it "a perfect unidirectional membrane: causal influences can cross it in only one direction". This means that events that occur inside the black hole cannot affect events that occur outside the black hole.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Finkelstein |first=D. |author-link1=David Finkelstein |date=1958 |title=Past-Future Asymmetry of the Gravitational Field of a Point Particle |journal=[[Physical Review]] | type=Article |volume=110 |issue=4 |pages=965–967 |bibcode=1958PhRv..110..965F |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.110.965}}</ref> Finkelstein created a new [[Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates|reference frame]] to include the point of view of infalling observers.<ref name="Bartusiak" />{{rp|103}} Finkelstein's new frame of reference allowed events at the surface of an imploding star to be related to events far away. By 1962 the two points of view were reconciled, convincing many sceptics that implosion into a black hole made physical sense.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|226}}

=== Golden age ===
[[File:BH-JPL-A&A1979.jpg|alt=A black-and-white image of a black hole with an accretion disk on punch cards. The black hole is visible as a black semicircle in the center with a white ring overlaid. Around it, a bright white accretion disk wraps around the top and bottom of the black hole and to its sides, appearing brightest on the left side of the black hole.|thumb|The first simulated image of a black hole, published by [[Jean-Pierre Luminet]] in 1979 and featuring the characteristic shadow, [[photon sphere]], and [[gravitational lensing|lensed]] [[accretion disk]]. The disk is brighter on one side due to [[Doppler beaming]].<ref>{{cite web |author=French National Centre for Scientific Research |title=First Ever Image of a Black Hole: A CNRS Researcher Had Simulated It as Early as 1979 |url=https://www.cnrs.fr/en/press/first-ever-image-black-hole-cnrs-researcher-had-simulated-it-early-1979 |website=CNRS |date=10 April 2019 |access-date=18 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260423213915/https://www.cnrs.fr/en/press/first-ever-image-black-hole-cnrs-researcher-had-simulated-it-early-1979 |archive-date=23 April 2026 |url-status=live}} Reports on paper: {{cite journal |last=Luminet |first=J.-P. |date=May 1979 |title=Image of a Spherical Black Hole with Thin Accretion Disk |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=75 |pages=228–235 |bibcode=1979A&A....75..228L }}</ref>]]

The era from the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s was the "golden age of black hole research", when general relativity and black holes became mainstream subjects of research.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Thorne |first1=Kip |author-link=Kip Thorne |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yLy4b61rfPwC |title=The Future of Theoretical Physics and Cosmology: Celebrating Stephen Hawking's 60th Birthday |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=2003 |isbn=0-521-82081-2 |veditors=Shellard ES, [[Gary Gibbons|Gibbons GW]], Rankin SJ |page=74 |chapter=5. Warping spacetime}}</ref><ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|p=258}}

In this period, solutions to the equations of general relativity under various different physical constraints were discovered. In 1963, [[Roy Kerr]] found [[Kerr metric|the exact solution]] for a [[rotating black hole]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Kerr |first=R. P. |author-link=Roy Kerr |title=The Kerr Spacetime |date=2009 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn=978-0-521-88512-6 |editor1-last=Wiltshire |editor1-first=D. L. |chapter=Discovering the Kerr and Kerr-Schild metrics |bibcode=2007arXiv0706.1109K |editor2-last=Visser |editor2-first=M. |editor3-last=Scott |editor3-first=S. M. |arxiv=0706.1109}}</ref> Two years later, [[Ezra T. Newman|Ezra Newman]] found the [[axisymmetric]] solution for a black hole that is both rotating and [[electrically charged]].<ref>{{cite journal |display-authors=2 |vauthors=[[Ezra T. Newman|Newman ET]], Couch E, Chinnapared K, Exton A, Prakash A, Torrence R |date=1965 |title=Metric of a Rotating, Charged Mass |journal=[[Journal of Mathematical Physics]] | type=Research article |volume=6 |issue=6 |page=918 |bibcode=1965JMP.....6..918N |doi=10.1063/1.1704351}}</ref>

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, scientists from research groups formed by [[Yakov Zeldovich]], [[John Archibald Wheeler]] and [[Dennis W. Sciama]] discovered a series of important mathematical properties of black hole models dubbed "a black hole has no hair" by Wheeler.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|272}} The first hints came from work by [[Vitaly Ginzburg]] who studied a series of increasing compact stars threaded with intense magnetic fields. He discovered that the fields get trapped on the black hole surface. In 1967, [[Werner Israel]] showed that any non-spinning, uncharged collapsing star gives a spherically symmetric black hole: any asymmetry must somehow vanish. In 1972, [[Richard H. Price]] found that the asymmetry was converted into gravitational waves. It took another 15 years and many physicists to produce a body of work that became known as the [[no-hair theorem]], which states that a stationary black hole is completely described by the three parameters of the [[Kerr–Newman metric]]: mass, angular momentum, and electric charge.<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|285}}

At first, it was suspected that the strange mathematical singularities found in each of the black hole solutions only appeared due to the assumption that a black hole would be perfectly [[Rotational symmetry#Rotational symmetry with respect to any angle|spherically symmetric]], and therefore the singularities would not appear in generic situations where black holes would not necessarily be symmetric. This view was held in particular by [[Vladimir Belinski]], [[Isaak Khalatnikov]], and [[Evgeny Lifshitz]], who tried to prove that no singularities appear in generic solutions, although they would later reverse their positions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Penrose |first1=Roger |author-link=Roger Penrose |date=1996 |title=Chandrasekhar, Black Holes, And Singularities |journal=[[Journal of Astrophysics and Astronomy]] | type=Article |volume=17 |issue=3–4 |pages=213–231 |bibcode=1996JApA...17..213P |doi=10.1007/BF02702305}}</ref> However, in 1965, [[Roger Penrose]] proved that general relativity predicts that singularities appear in all black holes,<ref name="penrose1965">{{cite journal |last1=Penrose |first1=R. |author-link1=Roger Penrose |date=1965 |title=Gravitational Collapse and Space-Time Singularities |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=14 |issue=3 |page=57 |bibcode=1965PhRvL..14...57P |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.14.57 }}</ref> although this may not still hold when [[quantum mechanics]] is taken into account.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ford |first1=L. H. |author1-link=Lawrence Ford |date=2003 |title=The Classical Singularity Theorems and Their Quantum Loopholes |journal=[[International Journal of Theoretical Physics]] | volume=42 |issue=6 |pages=1219–1227 |doi=10.1023/A:1025754515197 |arxiv=gr-qc/0301045 |bibcode=2003gr.qc.....1045F }}</ref>

Astronomical observations also made great strides during this era. In 1967, [[Antony Hewish]] and [[Jocelyn Bell Burnell]] discovered [[pulsar]]s, and by 1969 these were shown to be rapidly rotating neutron stars. Until that time, neutron stars, like black holes, were regarded as just theoretical curiosities, but the discovery of pulsars showed their physical relevance and spurred a further interest in all types of compact objects that might be formed by [[gravitational collapse]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/Fifty-years-ago-grad-students-discovery-changed-course-astrophysics-180968288/ |title=Fifty Years Ago, A Grad Student's Discovery Changed the Course of Astrophysics |date=28 February 2018 |access-date=22 December 2023 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |last=Boissoneault |first=Lorraine |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260223011330/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/Fifty-years-ago-grad-students-discovery-changed-course-astrophysics-180968288/ |archive-date=23 February 2026 |url-status=live}} Background and impact of {{cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Hewish |first1=A. |author-link1=Antony Hewish |last2=Bell |first2=S. J. |author-link2=Jocelyn Bell Burnell |last3=Pilkington |first3=J. D. H. |last4=Scott |first4=P. F. |last5=Collins |first5=R. A. |date=1968 |title=Observation of a Rapidly Pulsating Radio Source |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume=217 |issue=5130 |pages=709–713 |doi=10.1038/217709a0|bibcode=1968Natur.217..709H }}</ref> However, experimental evidence confirming a black hole was very difficult to obtain and ultimately required efforts from many astronomers. [[X-ray telescope]] observations by [[Riccardo Giacconi]]'s team in 1971 showed that [[Cygnus X-1]] emitted x-rays in rapid, sporadic fashion consistent with a compact source. This became the first candidate black hole.<ref name="Bartusiak" />{{rp|153}} Optical [[spectroscopy]] and detailed astrophysical models for Cygnus X-1 were consistent with a binary system of a massive star and compact star generating x-rays as gas from the massive but ordinary star was sucked into its invisible compact companion. (In 2011, the masses of these stars was estimated to be {{val|14.1|1.0|u=solar mass}} for the black hole and {{val|19.2|1.9|u=solar mass}} for the optical stellar companion.)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Orosz |first1=Jerome A. |last2=McClintock |first2=Jeffrey E. |last3=Aufdenberg |first3=Jason P. |last4=Remillard |first4=Ronald A. |last5=Reid |first5=Mark J. |last6=Narayan |first6=Ramesh |last7=Gou |first7=Lijun |display-authors=2 |title=The Mass of the Black Hole in Cygnus X-1 |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2011 |volume=742 |issue=2 |page=84 |doi=10.1088/0004-637x/742/2/84 |arxiv=1106.3689 |bibcode=2011ApJ...742...84O }}</ref> By 1974 the object was widely considered to be a black hole, but 100% confidence for Cygnus X-1 may not be possible.<ref name="Thorne-1994"/>{{rp|317}}

Work by [[James Bardeen]], [[Brandon Carter]], and [[Stephen Hawking]] in the early 1970s led to the formulation of [[black hole thermodynamics]]. These laws describe the behaviour of a black hole in a manner analogous to the [[laws of thermodynamics]]. [[Jacob Bekenstein]] strengthened this analogy with the properties of mass, [[surface area]], and [[surface gravity]] for a black hole related to the thermodynamical concepts of energy, [[entropy]], and [[temperature]] respectively. The analogy was completed<ref name="Thorne-1994" />{{rp|442}} when Hawking, in 1974, showed that [[quantum field theory]] implies that black holes should radiate like a [[black body]] with a temperature proportional to the surface gravity of the black hole, predicting the effect now known as [[Hawking radiation]].<ref name=Carlip-2015>{{cite book |last1=Carlip |first1=S. |title=Black hole thermodynamics |date=2017 |volume=2 |pages=415–465 |doi=10.1142/9789814678506_0010 |bibcode=2017ohy2.book..415C |isbn=978-981-4678-49-0 }} Discusses the history including {{cite journal |last1=Bardeen |first1=J. M. |author-link1=James M. Bardeen |last2=Carter |first2=B. |author-link2=Brandon Carter |last3=Hawking |first3=S. W. |author-link3=Stephen Hawking |date=1973 |title=The Four Laws of Black Hole Mechanics |journal=[[Communications in Mathematical Physics]] | volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=161–170 |doi=10.1007/BF01645742 |mr=0334798 |zbl=1125.83309 |bibcode=1973CMaPh..31..161B }} and {{cite journal |last=Hawking |first=S. W. |author-link1=Stephen Hawking |title=Black Hole Explosions? |journal=Nature |date=1974 |volume=248 |issue=5443 |pages=30–31 |doi=10.1038/248030a0 |bibcode=1974Natur.248...30H }}</ref>{{rp|415}}

=== Modern research and observation ===
[[File:LIGO measurement of gravitational waves.svg|upright=0.75|thumb|alt=Graphs of the first detections of gravitational waves at the Hanford and Livingston LIGO sections, along with comparisons to theoretical predictions, noise, and visual renderings. The readings appear as periodic waves that increase in magnitude over time before suddenly dropping back down.|The first detection of gravitational waves, imaged by [[LIGO]] observatories in [[Hanford Site]], Washington and [[Livingston, Louisiana]]]]While Cygnus X-1, a [[stellar-mass black hole]], was generally accepted by the scientific community as a black hole by the end of 1973,<ref name="rolston1997">{{cite web | last=Rolston | first=Bruce | date=10 November 1997 | url=http://news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/nov10_97/art4.htm | title=The First Black Hole | publisher=University of Toronto | access-date=11 March 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080307181205/http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/nov10_97/art4.htm | archive-date = 7 March 2008 }}</ref> it would be decades before a [[supermassive black hole]] would gain the same broad recognition. The idea that such objects might exist began with models suggesting that powerful [[quasar]]s or active galactic nuclei in the centre of galaxies were powered by [[accretion (astrophysics)|accreting]] supermassive black holes. When the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] launched in the 1990s, optical studies of the centre of galaxy [[Messier 87]] showed it must have a large concentration of mass. The two candidates for this mass were a black hole and a dense cluster of stars. In 1995, interferometric microwave spectra from the [[Very Long Baseline Array]] observed {{chem|H|2|O}} [[maser]]s as they orbited the centre of [[NGC 4258]], a galaxy with a similar central mass. The orbital parameters ruled out dense stellar clusters as an explanation for galactic nuclei, making supermassive black holes the only plausible explanation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scientific Background: Theoretical foundation for black holes and the supermassive compact object at the galactic centre |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2020/10/advanced-physicsprize2020.pdf |access-date=12 April 2026 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260619053209/https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2020/10/advanced-physicsprize2020.pdf |archive-date=19 June 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1999, [[David Merritt]] proposed the [[M–sigma relation]], which related the [[dispersion (statistics)|dispersion]] of the [[velocity]] of matter in the centre [[galactic bulge|bulge]] of a galaxy to the mass of the supermassive black hole at its core.<ref>{{cite conference | first = David | last = Merritt | author-link = David Merritt | editor1-first = F. | editor1-last = Combes | editor2-first = G. A. | editor2-last = Mamon | editor3-first = V. | editor3-last = Charmandaris | title = Black holes and galaxy evolution | volume = 197 | book-title = Dynamics of Galaxies: from the Early Universe to the Present | publisher = [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]] | pages = [https://archive.org/details/xvthiapmeetingdy0197iapm/page/221 221–232] | date = 1999 | isbn = 978-1-58381-024-8 | bibcode = 2000ASPC..197..221M | arxiv = astro-ph/9910546 | url = https://archive.org/details/xvthiapmeetingdy0197iapm/page/221 }}</ref> Subsequent studies confirmed this correlation.<ref>{{multiref2|{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Tremaine |first1=Scott | author1-link=Scott Tremaine |last2=Gebhardt |first2=Karl |last3=Bender |first3=Ralf |last4=Bower |first4=Gary |last5=Dressler |first5=Alan |last6=Faber |first6=S. M. |last7=Filippenko |first7=Alexei V. |last8=Green |first8=Richard |last9=Grillmair |first9=Carl |last10=Ho |first10=Luis C. |last11=Kormendy |first11=John |last12=Lauer |first12=Tod R. |last13=Magorrian |first13=John |last14=Pinkney |first14=Jason |last15=Richstone |first15=Douglas |title=The Slope of the Black Hole Mass Versus Velocity Dispersion Correlation |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2002 |volume=574 |issue=2 |pages=740–753 |doi=10.1086/341002 |arxiv=astro-ph/0203468 |bibcode=2002ApJ...574..740T }}|{{Cite journal |last1=Ferrarese |first1=Laura | author1-link=Laura Ferrarese |last2=Merritt |first2=David |title=A Fundamental Relation Between Supermassive Black Holes and Their Host Galaxies |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2000 |volume=539 |issue=1 |pages=L9–L12 |doi=10.1086/312838 |arxiv=astro-ph/0006053 |bibcode=2000ApJ...539L...9F }}|{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Nelson |first1=Charles H. |last2=Green |first2=Richard F. |last3=Bower |first3=Gary |last4=Gebhardt |first4=Karl |last5=Weistrop |first5=Donna |title=The Relationship Between Black Hole Mass and Velocity Dispersion in Seyfert 1 Galaxies |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2004 |volume=615 |issue=2 |pages=652–661 |doi=10.1086/424657 |arxiv=astro-ph/0407383 |bibcode=2004ApJ...615..652N }}}}</ref> Around the same time, based on telescope observations of the velocities of stars at the centre of the Milky Way galaxy, independent work groups led by [[Andrea Ghez]] and [[Reinhard Genzel]] concluded that the compact [[astronomical radio source|radio source]] in the centre of the galaxy, [[Sagittarius A*]], was likely a supermassive black hole.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Genzel |first1=R. |last2=Eckart |first2=A. |last3=Ott |first3=T. |last4=Eisenhauer |first4=F. |title=On the Nature of the Dark Mass in the Centre of the Milky Way |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=1997 |volume=291 |pages=219–234 |doi=10.1093/mnras/291.1.219 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Ghez1998" />

In late 2015, the [[LIGO Scientific Collaboration]] and [[Virgo Collaboration]] made the [[first observation of gravitational waves|first direct detection]] of [[gravitational wave]]s, named GW150914, representing the first observation of a [[black hole merger]].<ref name="PRL-20160211">{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=B. [[File:Black hole - Messier 87.jpg|thumb |alt=Over a black background of empty space, an orange-red donut of gas lies in the center of the image, with a black circle--the black hole's shadow--in the middle of the donut.|Image by the [[Event Horizon Telescope]] of the supermassive black hole in the centre of [[Messier 87]]]]

On 10 April 2019, the first direct image of a black hole and its vicinity was published, following observations made by the [[Event Horizon Telescope]] (EHT) of the supermassive black hole in [[Messier 87]]'s galactic centre.<ref name="APJL-20190410">{{cite journal|last1=Event Horizon Telescope|first1=The|author-link1=Event Horizon Telescope|date=2019|title=First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole|journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal]] | volume=875|page=L1|arxiv=1906.11238|bibcode=2019ApJ...875L...1E|doi=10.3847/2041-8213/ab0ec7|number=1 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released an image of the black hole in the center of the Milky Way galaxy, Sagittarius A*; the data had been collected in 2017.<ref name="eht-press-release" />

In 2020, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for work on black holes. [[Andrea Ghez]] and [[Reinhard Genzel]] shared one-half for their discovery that Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 Nobel Prize in Physics |url=https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/202011/nobel-physics.cfm |last=Poffenberger |first=Leah |access-date=20 October 2025 |website=American Physical Society |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260717204800/https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/202011/nobel-physics.cfm |archive-date=17 July 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> Penrose received the other half for his work showing that the mathematics of general relativity requires the formation of black holes.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2020|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/summary/|access-date=8 October 2020|website=NobelPrize.org|archive-date=24 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424115309/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2020/summary/|url-status=live}}</ref> Cosmologists lamented that Hawking's extensive theoretical work on black holes would not be honoured, since he had died in 2018 and the Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Overbye |first1=Dennis |author-link1=Dennis Overbye |last2=Taylor |first2=Derrick Bryson |title=Nobel Prize in Physics Awarded to 3 Scientists for Work on Black Holes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/06/science/nobel-prize-physics.html |date=6 October 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=6 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201006102031/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/06/science/nobel-prize-physics.html |archive-date=6 October 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
In December 1967, someone in the audience reportedly suggested the phrase ''black hole'' at a lecture by [[John Archibald Wheeler|John Wheeler]]; Wheeler adopted the term for its brevity and "advertising value", and Wheeler's stature in the field ensured it quickly caught on,<ref name="Bartusiak" /><ref>{{cite news |title=Pioneering Physicist John Wheeler Dies at 96 |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/pioneering-physicist-john-wheeler-dies/ |access-date=27 November 2016 |work=[[Scientific American]] | url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161128050759/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/pioneering-physicist-john-wheeler-dies/ |archive-date=28 November 2016}}</ref> leading some to credit Wheeler with coining the phrase.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Overbye |first1=Dennis |title=John A. Wheeler, Physicist Who Coined the Term 'Black Hole,' Is Dead at 96 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/14/science/14wheeler.html |access-date=27 November 2016 |work=[[The New York Times]] | date=14 April 2008 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122210005/http://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/14/science/14wheeler.html |archive-date=22 November 2016}}</ref> However, the term was used by others around that time. Science writer Marcia Bartusiak traces the term ''black hole'' to physicist [[Robert H. Dicke]], who in the early 1960s reportedly compared the phenomenon to the [[Black Hole of Calcutta]], notorious as a prison where people entered but never left alive. The term was used in print by ''[[Life (magazine)|Life]]'' and ''[[Science News]]'' magazines in 1963, and by science journalist Ann Ewing in her article {{" '}}Black Holes' in Space", dated 18 January 1964, which was a report on a meeting of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] held in Cleveland, Ohio.<ref name="Bartusiak">{{cite book |last=Bartusiak |first=Marcia |author-link=Marcia Bartusiak |title=Black Hole: How an Idea Abandoned by Newtonians, Hated by Einstein, And Gambled On by Hawking Became Loved |date=2015 |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] | isbn=978-0-300-21363-8}}</ref>

== Definition ==
A black hole is generally defined as a region of spacetime from which no [[Randomness#In the physical sciences|information-carrying]] signals or objects can escape.<ref name="fz11">{{Cite book |title=Introduction to Black Hole Physics |last1=Frolov |first1=Valeri P. |date=1 December 2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-969229-3 |edition=1st |page=1 |last2=Zelnikov |first2=Andrei}}</ref> However, verifying an object as a black hole by this definition would require waiting for an infinite time and at an infinite distance from the black hole to verify that nothing has escaped, and thus cannot be used to identify a physical black hole.<ref name="booth05">{{Cite journal |last1=Booth |first1=Ivan |title=Black-hole boundaries |journal=Canadian Journal of Physics |date=2005 |volume=83 |issue=11 |pages=1073–1099 |doi=10.1139/p05-063 |arxiv=gr-qc/0508107 |bibcode=2005CaJPh..83.1073B }}</ref> There are several other definitions that can be used to describe or identify black holes, leading to a variety of ways to study them. Astronomical observations measure the mass of objects, and gravitational collapse theories predict that a [[compact object]] with a mass larger than three solar masses can only be a black hole: this limit has become the observational definition.<ref name="curiel19">{{Cite journal |last1=Curiel |first1=Erik |title=The many definitions of a black hole |journal=Nature Astronomy |date=2019 |volume=3 |pages=27–34 |doi=10.1038/s41550-018-0602-1 |arxiv=1808.01507 |bibcode=2019NatAs...3...27C }}</ref> A black hole may also be defined as a reservoir of information<ref name="bhwar">{{cite book |last=Susskind |first=Leonard |author-link=Leonard Susskind |title=The black hole war: my battle with Stephen Hawking to make the world safe for quantum mechanics |title-link=The Black Hole War |date=2008 |publisher=Little, Brown |isbn=978-0-316-01640-7 |edition=1st |oclc=181603165}}</ref>{{rp|142}} or a region where space is falling inwards faster than the speed of light.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hamilton |first1=Andrew J. S. |last2=Lisle |first2=Jason P. |title=The river model of black holes |journal=American Journal of Physics |date=2008 |volume=76 |issue=6 |pages=519–532 |doi=10.1119/1.2830526 |arxiv=gr-qc/0411060 |bibcode=2008AmJPh..76..519H }}</ref><ref name="waterfall">{{Cite web |title=A Black Hole is a Waterfall of Space |url=https://jila.colorado.edu/~ajsh/insidebh/waterfall.html |last=Hamilton |first=Andrew |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250820063124/https://jila.colorado.edu/%7Eajsh/insidebh/waterfall.html |archive-date=20 August 2025 |access-date=24 October 2025 |website=Inside Black Holes}}</ref>

== Properties ==
The [[no-hair theorem]] establishes that, once it achieves a stable condition after formation, a black hole has only three independent physical properties: mass, electric charge, and angular momentum; the black hole is otherwise featureless. Any two black holes that share the same values for these properties, or parameters, are indistinguishable from one another. A related ''no-hair conjecture'' proposes that dynamic gravitational collapse always results in an object characterized with only these three properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Herdeiro |first1=Carlos A. R. |last2=Radu |first2=Eugen |title=Asymptotically flat black holes with scalar hair: A review |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D |date=2015 |volume=24 |issue=9 |pages=1542014–1542219 |doi=10.1142/S0218271815420146 |arxiv=1504.08209 |bibcode=2015IJMPD..2442014H }}</ref> The conjecture is currently an unsolved problem.<ref name="HeuslerNoHair">{{cite journal |vauthors=Chruściel PT, Costa JL, Heusler M |date=2012 |title=Stationary Black Holes: Uniqueness and Beyond |journal=[[Living Reviews in Relativity]] | type=Article |volume=15 |issue=7 |arxiv=1205.6112 |bibcode=2012LRR....15....7C |doi=10.12942/lrr-2012-7 |pmc=5255892 |pmid=28179837 |doi-access=free |article-number=7}}</ref> The no-hair theorem also makes idealized assumptions in addition to equilibrium that may not apply to astrophysical objects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barceló |first1=Carlos |last2=Carballo-Rubio |first2=Raúl |last3=Garay |first3=Luis J |last4=García-Moreno |first4=Gerardo |date=31 March 2025 |title=No-hair and almost-no-hair results for static axisymmetric black holes and ultracompact objects in astrophysical environments  |journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity |volume=42 |issue=7 |pages=075020 |doi=10.1088/1361-6382/adc233 |arxiv=2410.08128 |bibcode=2025CQGra..42g5020B }}</ref>

The simplest equilibrium black hole model with only mass but neither electric charge nor angular momentum is called a ''Schwarzschild black hole''. Non-rotating [[charged black hole]]s are described by the [[Reissner–Nordström metric]], while the [[Kerr metric]] describes a non-charged [[rotating black hole]]. The most general [[stationary spacetime|stationary]] black hole solution known is the [[Kerr–Newman metric]], which describes a black hole with both charge and angular momentum.<ref name="shapiro_teukolsky1983">{{cite book |last1=Shapiro |first1=S. L. |last2=Teukolsky |first2=S. A. |author2-link=Saul Teukolsky |title=Black Holes, White Dwarfs, And Neutron Stars: The Physics of Compact Objects |page=357 |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |date=1983 |isbn=978-0-471-87316-7}}</ref>

=== Mass ===
[[File:Black Hole Shadow.ogg|thumbtime=0|thumb|alt=A black hole's Schwarzschild radius is described by the equation r sub s equals two G M over c squared. The radius of its shadow is described by the equation R equals square root of 27 over 2 r sub s approximately equals 2.6 r sub s. The radius of its photon sphere is described by the equation R equals 1.5 r sub s.|Radii for shadow and photon sphere relative to the event horizon]]

The simplest static black holes have mass but neither electric charge nor angular momentum. Contrary to the popular notion of a black hole "sucking in everything" in its surroundings, from far away, the external gravitational field of a black hole is identical to that of any other body of the same mass.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Michael A. |last1=Seeds |first2=Dana E. |last2=Backman |title=Perspectives on Astronomy |page=167 |publisher=Cengage Learning |date=2007 |isbn=978-0-495-11352-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CXom04KGIL8C&pg=PA167|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160810211808/https://books.google.com/books?id=CXom04KGIL8C&pg=PA167 |archive-date=10 August 2016}}</ref>

While a black hole can theoretically have any positive mass, its charge and angular momentum are limited by its mass, with this limit being greater for more massive black holes. The net electric charge <math>Q</math> and the total angular momentum <math>J</math> satisfy the inequality
<math display="block">\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} + \frac{c^2 J^2}{G M^2} \le G M^2</math>
for a black hole of mass <math>M</math>, where <math>\epsilon_0</math> is the [[vacuum permittivity]] constant, <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]] and <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]]. Black holes with the maximum possible combination of charge and spin satisfying this inequality are called [[extremal black hole]]s. Adding a low-mass object with a lot of charge or angular momentum to an extremal black hole would create a so-called [[naked singularity]], a singularity outside of a black hole.<ref name="wald 1997">{{cite book |last=Wald |first=R. M. |author-link=Robert Wald |title=Black Holes, Gravitational Radiation and the Universe |editor1=Iyer, B. R. |editor2=Bhawal, B. |chapter=Gravitational Collapse and Cosmic Censorship |arxiv=gr-qc/9710068 |date=1997 |pages=69–86|publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-0934-7 |isbn=978-94-017-0934-7}}</ref> Because these singularities make the [[universe]] inherently unpredictable, many physicists believe they could not exist.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Berger |first=B. K.|author-link= Beverly Berger |date=2002 |title=Numerical Approaches to Spacetime Singularities |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=2002–1|article-number=1 |bibcode=2002LRR.....5....1B |doi=10.12942/lrr-2002-1 |doi-access=free |pmid=28179859 |pmc=5256073 |arxiv=gr-qc/0201056}}</ref> The [[weak cosmic censorship hypothesis]], proposed by Penrose, rules out the formation of such singularities, when they are created through the gravitational collapse of [[energy conditions|realistic matter]]. This hypothesis remains an important area of study because has not yet been proven and it relates to many aspects of general relativity and [[quantum gravity]].<ref name="joshi09">{{Cite magazine |date=1 February 2009 |title=Naked Singularities |magazine=[[Scientific American]] | last=Joshi |first=Pankaj S.  |pages=36–43 |volume=300 |issue=2 |jstor=26001219 }}</ref>

The total mass of a nearby black hole can be estimated by analysing the motion of the stars or gas surrounding it. The mass of distant supermassive black holes can be inferred from [[Doppler broadening]] of spectral lines emitted by rapidly orbiting gas, a technique called [[reverberation mapping]].<ref name="peterson14" />

=== Spin and angular momentum ===
All black holes spin, often rapidly. One stellar black hole, [[GRS 1915+105]], has been estimated to spin at over 1,000 revolutions per second.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Black Hole Basics |url=https://science.nasa.gov/universe/black-holes/ |access-date=25 October 2025 |website=NASA.gov |date=13 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260822160930/https://science.nasa.gov/universe/black-holes/ |archive-date=22 August 2026 |url-status=live }}</ref> The Milky Way's central black hole Sagittarius A* rotates at about 90% of the maximum possible rate.<ref name="daly19">{{Cite journal |last1=Daly |first1=Ruth A. |title=Black Hole Spin and Accretion Disk Magnetic Field Strength Estimates for More Than 750 Active Galactic Nuclei and Multiple Galactic Black Holes |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2019 |volume=886 |issue=1 |page=37 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/ab35e6 |arxiv=1905.11319 |bibcode=2019ApJ...886...37D |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The spin rate can be inferred from measurements of atomic [[spectral line]]s in the X-ray range. As gas near the black hole plunges inward, high energy X-ray emission from electron-positron pairs illuminates the gas further out, appearing red-shifted due to relativistic effects. Depending on the spin of the black hole, this plunge happens at different radii from the hole, with different degrees of redshift. Astronomers can use the gap between the x-ray emission of the outer disk and the redshifted emission from plunging material to determine the spin of the black hole.<ref name="reynolds19">{{cite journal |last1=Reynolds |first1=Christopher S. |title=Observing black holes spin |journal=Nature Astronomy |date=2019 |volume=3 |pages=41–47 |doi=10.1038/s41550-018-0665-z |arxiv=1903.11704 |bibcode=2019NatAs...3...41R }}</ref>

A newer way to estimate spin is based on the temperature of gases accreting onto the black hole. The method requires an independent measurement of the black hole mass and [[inclination angle]] of the accretion disk followed by computer modelling. Gravitational waves from coalescing binary black holes can also provide the spin of both progenitor black holes and the merged hole, but such events are rare.<ref name="reynolds19" />

A spinning black hole has [[angular momentum]]. The [[Kerr metric]] is the solution of [[Einstein's field equations]] for a rotating black hole. In addition to the [[Schwarzschild radius]], <math>r_\textrm{S}</math>, it includes a rotational parameter,
<math display="block">a = \frac{J}{M} = \frac{2J}{r_\textrm{S}},
</math>where <math>J</math> is the black hole angular momentum. An extremal black hole has <math>|J|= M^2</math>, corresponding to <math>a=1</math>.<ref name=Zee-2013>{{Cite book |last=Zee |first=A. |title=Einstein gravity in a nutshell |date=2013 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-14558-7 |location=Princeton}}</ref>{{rp|467}} The supermassive black hole in the centre of the [[Messier 87]] (M87) galaxy appears to have rotational parameter of {{val|0.90|0.05}}, very close to the maximum theoretical value.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tamburini |first1=Fabrizio |last2=Thidé |first2=Bo |last3=Della Valle |first3=Massimo |title=Measurement of the Spin of the M87 Black Hole from Its Observed Twisted Light |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society: Letters |date=2020 |volume=492 |pages=L22–L27 |doi=10.1093/mnrasl/slz176 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1904.07923 }}</ref>

=== Charge ===
Black holes are believed to have an approximately neutral charge. For example, Michal Zajaček, Arman Tursunov, Andreas Eckart, and Silke Britzen found the [[electric charge]] of Sagittarius A* to be at least ten orders of magnitude below the theoretical maximum.<ref name="zteb18" /> If a black hole were to become charged, particles with an opposite sign of charge would be pulled in by the extra [[electromagnetic force]], while particles with the same sign of charge would be repelled, neutralising the black hole. This effect operates even more rapidly if the black hole is also spinning.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Gong |first1=Yi |last2=Cao |first2=Zhoujian |last3=Gao |first3=He |last4=Zhang |first4=Bing |title=On Neutralization of Charged Black Holes |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2019 |volume=488 |issue=2 |pages=2722–2731 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stz1904 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1907.05239 |quote=We find a universal dependence of the falling probability into the black hole on the charge of the test particle, with the oppositely charged particles having a higher probability of falling.}}</ref> A spinning black hole in a magnetic field creates an [[electric field]] which would interact with charged particles.<ref name="zteb18">{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Zajaček |first1=Michal |last2=Tursunov |first2=Arman |last3=Eckart |first3=Andreas |last4=Britzen |first4=Silke |title=On the Charge of the Galactic Centre Black Hole |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2018 |volume=480 |issue=4 |pages=4408–4423 |doi=10.1093/mnras/sty2182 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1808.07327 }}</ref> Since black holes have so few measurable intrinsic properties, techniques for measuring charge are of interest to astrophysics even if the values may be very small.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Zakharov |first1=A. F. |last2=De Paolis |first2=F. |last3=Ingrosso |first3=G. |last4=Nucita |first4=A. A. |title=Direct Measurements of Black Hole Charge with Future Astrometrical Missions |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |date=2005 |volume=442 |issue=3 |pages=795–799 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20053432  |doi-access=free|arxiv=astro-ph/0505286 |bibcode=2005A&A...442..795Z }}</ref>

The charge Q for a nonspinning black hole is bounded by
<math display="block">Q\leq\sqrt{4\pi \epsilon_0 G}M,</math>
where G is the gravitational constant and M is the black hole's mass.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Turimov |first1=Bobur |last2=Boboqambarova |first2=Madina |last3=Ahmedov |first3=Bobomurat |last4=Stuchlík |first4=Zdeněk |title=Distinguishable Feature of Electric and Magnetic Charged Black Hole |journal=The European Physical Journal Plus |date=2022 |volume=137 |issue=2 |article-number=222 |doi=10.1140/epjp/s13360-022-02390-7}}</ref>

Black holes are classified by the theory of their formation and by their mass (expressed in terms of {{solar mass}}, the mass of the Sun), but these criteria are intertwined. [[Stellar black hole]]s are formed by stellar collapse. The minimum mass of a black hole formed by stellar gravitational collapse is governed by the maximum mass of a neutron star and is believed to be {{solar mass|2-4}}.<ref>{{multiref2 |{{Cite journal |last1=Drischler |first1=Christian |last2=Han |first2=Sophia |last3=Lattimer |first3=James M. |last4=Prakash |first4=Madappa |last5=Reddy |first5=Sanjay |last6=Zhao |first6=Tianqi |title=Limiting Masses and Radii of Neutron Stars and Their Implications |journal=Physical Review C |date=2021 |volume=103 |issue=4 |article-number=045808 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.103.045808 |arxiv=2009.06441 |bibcode=2021PhRvC.103d5808D |display-authors=2}}|{{Cite journal |last1=Farr |first1=Will M. |last2=Sravan |first2=Niharika |last3=Cantrell |first3=Andrew |last4=Kreidberg |first4=Laura |last5=Bailyn |first5=Charles D. |last6=Mandel |first6=Ilya |last7=Kalogera |first7=Vicky |title=The Mass Distribution of Stellar-Mass Black Holes |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2011 |volume=741 |issue=2 |page=103 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/741/2/103 |arxiv=1011.1459 |bibcode=2011ApJ...741..103F |display-authors=2}}}}</ref> Hypothetical [[primordial black hole]]s, believed to have formed soon after the [[Big Bang]], could be far smaller, with masses as little as {{val|e=-5|u=grams}} at formation.<ref name="Carr">{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Carr |first1=Bernard |last2=Kohri |first2=Kazunori |last3=Sendouda |first3=Yuuiti |last4=Yokoyama |first4=Jun'Ichi |title=Constraints on Primordial Black Holes |journal=Reports on Progress in Physics |date=2021 |volume=84 |issue=11 |doi=10.1088/1361-6633/ac1e31 |pmid=34874316 |arxiv=2002.12778 |bibcode=2021RPPh...84k6902C }}</ref> These very small black holes are sometimes called [[micro black hole]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nakama |first1=Tomohiro |last2=Yokoyama |first2=Jun'Ichi |title=Micro Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe and Their Cosmological Implications |journal=Physical Review D |date=2019 |volume=99 |issue=6 |article-number=061303 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.99.061303 |arxiv=1811.05049 |bibcode=2019PhRvD..99f1303N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Scardigli |first1=Fabio |title=Gravity Coupling from Micro-Black Holes |journal=Nuclear Physics B: Proceedings Supplements |date=2000 |volume=88 |issue=1–3 |pages=291–294 |doi=10.1016/S0920-5632(00)00788-X |arxiv=hep-th/9907150 |bibcode=2000NuPhS..88..291S }}</ref>

Stellar black holes can have a wide range of masses. Estimates of their maximum mass at formation vary, but generally range from {{solar mass|10-100}}, with higher estimates for black holes progenated by [[metallicity|low-metallicity]] stars.<ref name=Vink-2021>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Vink |first1=Jorick S. |last2=Higgins |first2=Erin R. |last3=Sander |first3=Andreas A C. |last4=Sabhahit |first4=Gautham N. |title=Maximum Black Hole Mass Across Cosmic Time |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2021 |volume=504 |pages=146–154 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stab842 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2010.11730 }}</ref> Stellar black holes can gain mass via accretion of nearby matter, often from a companion object such as a star<ref name="lph97">{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Dunn |first1=R. J. H. |last2=Fender |first2=R. P. |last3=Körding |first3=E. G. |last4=Belloni |first4=T. |last5=Cabanac |first5=C. |title=A Global Spectral Study of Black Hole X-Ray Binaries |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2010 |volume=403 |issue=1 |pages=61–82 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2010.16114.x |arxiv=0912.0142 |bibcode=2010MNRAS.403...61D |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shao |first1=Yong |last2=Li |first2=Xiang-Dong |title=Population Synthesis of Black Hole X-Ray Binaries |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2020 |volume=898 |issue=2 |page=143 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/aba118 |arxiv=2006.15961 |bibcode=2020ApJ...898..143S |doi-access=free }}</ref> or by merger with another black hole.<ref name="PRL-20160211"/>

A small number of candidate black holes with masses in the range {{solar mass|{{value|e=2}}-{{value|e=4}}}} have been reported. These are larger than stellar black holes but smaller than supermassive black holes, are rarer than either extreme, and are called [[intermediate-mass black hole]]s.<ref name="mc04">{{Cite journal |last1=Coleman Miller |first1=M. |last2=Colbert |first2=E. J. M. |title=Intermediate-Mass Black Holes |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D |date=2004 |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=1–64 |doi=10.1142/S0218271804004426 |arxiv=astro-ph/0308402 |bibcode=2004IJMPD..13....1M }}</ref> Physicists have speculated that such black holes may form from collisions in [[globular]] and [[star cluster]]s or at the centre of [[dwarf galaxy|low-mass galaxies]].<ref>{{multiref2|{{Cite journal |last1=Coleman Miller |first1=M. |last2=Hamilton |first2=Douglas P. |title=Production of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes in Globular Clusters |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2002 |volume=330 |issue=1 |pages=232–240 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-8711.2002.05112.x |arxiv=astro-ph/0106188 |bibcode=2002MNRAS.330..232C |doi-access=free }}|{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Rizzuto |first1=Francesco Paolo |last2=Naab |first2=Thorsten |last3=Spurzem |first3=Rainer |last4=Giersz |first4=Mirek |last5=Ostriker |first5=J. P. |last6=Stone |first6=N. C. |last7=Wang |first7=Long |last8=Berczik |first8=Peter |last9=Rampp |first9=M. |title=Intermediate Mass Black Hole Formation in Compact Young Massive Star Clusters |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2021 |volume=501 |issue=4 |pages=5257–5273 |doi=10.1093/mnras/staa3634 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2008.09571 }}|{{Cite journal |last1=Barai |first1=Paramita |last2=De Gouveia Dal Pino |first2=Elisabete M. |title=Intermediate-Mass Black Hole Growth and Feedback in Dwarf Galaxies at High Redshifts |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2019 |volume=487 |issue=4 |pages=5549–5563 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stz1616 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1807.04768 }}}}</ref> They may also form as the result of mergers of smaller black holes, with several gravitational wave measurements consistent with merged black holes within {{solar mass|110–350}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Ruiz-Rocha |first1=Krystal |last2=Yelikar |first2=Anjali B. |last3=Lange |first3=Jacob |last4=Gabella |first4=William |last5=Weller |first5=Robert A. |last6=o'Shaughnessy |first6=Richard |last7=Holley-Bockelmann |first7=Kelly |last8=Jani |first8=Karan |title=Properties of "Lite" Intermediate-Mass Black Hole Candidates in LIGO-Virgo's Third Observing Run |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters |date=2025 |volume=985 |issue=2 |pages=L37 |doi=10.3847/2041-8213/adc5f8 |arxiv=2502.17681 |bibcode=2025ApJ...985L..37R |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The black holes with the largest masses are called [[supermassive black hole]]s, with masses more than {{solar mass|{{value|e=6}}}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mezcua |first1=Mar |title=Encyclopedia of Astrobiology |chapter=Black Holes |date=2021 |pages=1–8 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-27833-4_5510-1 |arxiv=2110.08629 |isbn=978-3-642-27833-4 }}</ref> These black holes are believed to exist at the centres of almost every large galaxy, including the Milky Way.<ref name=Cattaneo-2009/> Some scientists have proposed a subcategory of even larger black holes, called [[ultramassive black hole]]s, with masses greater than {{solar mass|{{value|e=9}}-{{value|e=10}}}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Natarajan |first1=Priyamvada |last2=Treister |first2=Ezequiel |title=Is There an Upper Limit to Black Hole Masses? |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2009 |volume=393 |issue=3 |pages=838–845 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2008.13864.x |arxiv=0808.2813 |bibcode=2009MNRAS.393..838N |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dullo |first1=Bililign T. |last2=Gil De Paz |first2=Armando |last3=Knapen |first3=Johan H. |title=Ultramassive Black Holes in the Most Massive Galaxies: M <sub>BH</sub>–σ Versus M <sub>BH</sub>–R <sub>b</sub> |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2021 |volume=908 |issue=2 |page=134 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/abceae |arxiv=2012.04471 |bibcode=2021ApJ...908..134D |doi-access=free }}</ref> Theoretical models predict that the accretion disc that feeds black holes will be unstable once a black hole reaches {{solar mass|{{val|50|e=9}}–{{val|100|e=9}}}}, setting a rough upper limit to black hole mass.<ref>{{cite journal | title=How big can a black hole grow? | last1=King | first1=Andrew | journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society: Letters | volume=456 | issue=1 | pages=L109–L112 | date=February 2016 | doi=10.1093/mnrasl/slv186 | doi-access=free | bibcode=2016MNRAS.456L.109K | arxiv=1511.08502 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clery |first1=Daniel |title=Limit to how big black holes can grow is astonishing |journal=Science |date=21 December 2015 |doi=10.1126/science.aae0149 }}</ref>

== Structure ==

While black holes are conceptually invisible sinks of all matter and light, in astronomical settings, their enormous gravity alters the motion of surrounding objects and pulls nearby gas inwards at near-light speed, making the area around black holes the brightest objects in the universe.<ref name="reynolds21">{{cite journal |last1=Reynolds |first1=Christopher S. |title=Observational Constraints on Black Hole Spin |journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics |date=2021 |volume=59 |pages=117–154 |doi=10.1146/annurev-astro-112420-035022 |arxiv=2011.08948 |bibcode=2021ARA&A..59..117R }}</ref>

=== External geometry ===
==== Relativistic jets ====
{{See also|Astrophysical jet}}
[[File:Black Hole Outflows From Centaurus A.jpg|thumb |alt=See caption. |Relativistic jets from the supermassive black hole in [[Centaurus A]] extend [[perpendicular]]ly from the galaxy.]]
Some black holes have relativistic jets—thin streams of [[plasma (physics)|plasma]] travelling away from the black hole at more than 90% of the speed of light.<ref name="mr99">{{Cite journal |last1=Mirabel |first1=I. F. |last2=Rodríguez |first2=L. F. |title=Sources of Relativistic Jets in the Galaxy |journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics |date=1999 |volume=37 |pages=409–443 |doi=10.1146/annurev.astro.37.1.409 |arxiv=astro-ph/9902062 |bibcode=1999ARA&A..37..409M }}</ref> A small fraction of the matter falling towards the black hole gets accelerated away along the hole rotation axis.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Relativistic Jets |url=https://nustar.caltech.edu/page/relativistic-jets |access-date=9 November 2025 |website=NuSTAR |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260419114356/https://nustar.caltech.edu/page/relativistic-jets |archive-date=19 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> These jets can extend as far as millions of [[light-year]]s from the black hole itself.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last9=Jacob |first9=Joe |last1=Bagchi |first1=Joydeep |last2=Vivek |first2=M. |last3=Vikram |first3=Vinu |last4=Hota |first4=Ananda |last5=Biju |first5=K. G. |last6=Sirothia |first6=S. K. |last7=Srianand |first7=Raghunathan |last8=Gopal-Krishna |title=Megaparsec Relativistic Jets Launched from an Accreting Supermassive Black Hole in an Extreme Spiral Galaxy |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2014 |volume=788 |issue=2 |page=174 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/788/2/174 |arxiv=1404.6889 |bibcode=2014ApJ...788..174B }}</ref>

Black holes of any mass can have jets.<ref name="nemmen12">{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1= Nemmen|first1= R. S.|last2= Georganopoulos|first2= M.|last3= Guiriec|first3= S.|last4= Meyer|first4= E. T.|last5= Gehrels|first5= N.|last6= Sambruna|first6= R. M.|title=A Universal Scaling for the Energetics of Relativistic Jets from Black Hole Systems|journal= Science|date= 2012|volume= 338|issue= 6113|pages= 1445–1448|doi= 10.1126/science.1227416|pmid= 23239730|arxiv= 1212.3343|bibcode= 2012Sci...338.1445N}}</ref> However, they are typically observed around spinning black holes with strongly-magnetized accretion disks.<ref name="bmr18">{{Cite journal |last1=Blandford |first1=Roger |last2=Meier |first2=David |last3=Readhead |first3=Anthony |title=Relativistic Jets from Active Galactic Nuclei |journal=Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics |date=2019 |volume=57 |pages=467–509 |doi=10.1146/annurev-astro-081817-051948 |arxiv=1812.06025 |bibcode=2019ARA&A..57..467B }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Chen 陈 |first1=Yongyun 永云 |last2=Gu 顾 |first2=Qiusheng 秋生 |last3=Fan 樊 |first3=Junhui 军辉 |last4=Zhou 周 |first4=Hongyan 宏岩 |last5=Yuan 袁 |first5=Yefei 业飞 |last6=Gu 顾 |first6=Weimin 为民 |last7=Wu 吴 |first7=Qinwen 庆文 |last8=Xiong 熊 |first8=Dingrong 定荣 |last9=Guo 郭 |first9=Xiaotong 晓通 |last10=Ding 丁 |first10=Nan 楠. |last11=Yu 俞 |first11=Xiaoling 效龄 |title=The Powers of Relativistic Jets Depend on the Spin of Accreting Supermassive Black Holes |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=2021 |volume=913 |issue=2 |page=93 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/abf4ff |arxiv=2104.04242 |bibcode=2021ApJ...913...93C |doi-access=free }}</ref> Relativistic jets were more common in the [[Chronology of the universe#Gravity builds cosmic structure|early universe]], when galaxies and their corresponding supermassive black holes were rapidly gaining mass.<ref name="bmr18" /><ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Ghisellini |first1=G. |last2=Haardt |first2=F. |last3=Ceca |first3=R. Della |last4=Volonteri |first4=M. |last5=Sbarrato |first5=T. |title=The Role of Relativistic Jets in the Heaviest and Most Active Supermassive Black Holes at High Redshift |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=2013 |volume=432 |issue=4 |pages=2818–2823 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stt637 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1304.1152 }}</ref> All black holes with jets also have an accretion disk,<ref name="mr99" /> but the jets are usually brighter than the disk.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=2 |last1=Ghisellini |first1=G. |last2=Tavecchio |first2=F. |last3=Maraschi |first3=L. |last4=Celotti |first4=A. |last5=Sbarrato |first5=T. |title=The Power of Relativistic Jets Is Larger Than the Luminosity of Their Accretion Disks |journal=Nature |date=2014 |volume=515 |issue=7527 |pages=376–378 |doi=10.1038/nature13856 |pmid=25409827 |arxiv=1411.5368 |bibcode=2014Natur.515..376G }}</ref> ''[[Quasar]]s,'' typically found in other galaxies, are believed to be supermassive black holes with jets; ''[[microquasar]]s'' are believed to be stellar-mass objects with jets, typically observed in the Milky Way.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mirabel |first1=I. F. |last2=Rodríguez |first2=L. F. |title=Microquasars in our Galaxy |journal=Nature |date=1998 |volume=392 |issue=6677 |pages=673–676 |doi=10.1038/33603 |bibcode=1998Natur.392..673M }}</ref>

The jets can be powered by either the accretion disk or the rotating black hole spin. While many details of the jets have been studied, no complete model has emerged.  One method proposed to fuel these jets is the [[Blandford-Znajek process]], which suggests that the dragging of [[magnetic field lines]] by a black hole's rotation could launch jets of matter into space.<ref name="bmr18" /> The [[Penrose process]], which involves extraction of a black hole's [[rotational energy]], has also been proposed as a potential mechanism of jet propulsion.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Penrose |first1=R. |year=1969
|title=Gravitational Collapse: The Role of General Relativity |journal=[[Rivista del Nuovo Cimento]] | volume=1 |pages=252–276 |bibcode=1969NCimR...1..252P}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Narayan |first1=Ramesh |last2=McClintock |first2=Jeffrey E. |last3=Tchekhovskoy |first3=Alexander |title=General Relativity, Cosmology and Astrophysics |chapter=Energy Extraction from Spinning Black Holes Via Relativistic Jets |date=2014 |pages=523–535 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-06349-2_25 |arxiv=1303.3004 |isbn=978-3-319-06348-5 }}</ref> There is evidence that jets at all scales, from microquasars to [[gamma ray burst]]s may be produced by a single mechanism.<ref name="nemmen12" />

==== Accretion disk ====
{{Main|Accretion disk}}

[[File:Black Hole Desktop & Phone Wallpapers (SVS14146 - BH accretion disk viz desktop).png|thumb|alt=An black hole with an orange-red accretion disk. The disk is wrapped around the black hole in a ring across its center and semicircles around the top and bottom of the black hole. The semicircles are actually the part of the accretion disk that is behind the black hole, and appears gravitationally lensed to be above and below the hole.|Visualization of a black hole with an orange accretion disk. The parts of the disk circling over and under the hole are actually gravitationally lensed from the back side of the black hole.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Black Hole Anatomy |url=https://science.nasa.gov/universe/black-holes/anatomy/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250424044622/https://science.nasa.gov/universe/black-holes/anatomy/ |archive-date=24 April 2025 |access-date=13 October 2025 |website=NASA Science |date=2 August 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cunha |first1=Pedro V.P. |last2=Eiró |first2=Nelson A. |last3=Herdeiro |first3=Carlos A.R. |last4=Lemos |first4=José P.S. |title=Lensing and shadow of a black hole surrounded by a heavy accretion disk |journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics |date=2020 |issue=3 |page=035 |doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2020/03/035 |arxiv=1912.08833 |bibcode=2020JCAP...03..035C }}</ref>]]
Due to [[conservation of angular momentum]], gas falling into the [[gravitational well]] created by a massive object will typically form a disk-like structure around the object.<ref>{{cite book |title=Astrophysics |series=Undergraduate Lecture Notes in Physics |date=2024 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-22135-4 |isbn=978-3-031-22133-0 }}</ref>{{rp|242}} As the disk's angular momentum is transferred outward due to processes such as turbulence in the disk, its matter falls farther inward, converting its gravitational energy into heat and releasing a large amount of radiation; absent an explosive event, the radiation pressure [[Eddington limit|limits the accretion rate]].<ref name="High-Energy Astrophysics">{{cite book |title=High-Energy Astrophysics |series=Undergraduate Lecture Notes in Physics |date=2022 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-92159-0 |isbn=978-3-030-92158-3 }}</ref>{{rp|165}} The temperature of these disks can range from thousands to millions of [[kelvin]]s, and temperatures differ throughout a single accretion disk.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lasota |first1=Jean-Pierre |title=Astrophysics of Black Holes |chapter=Black Hole Accretion Discs |series=Astrophysics and Space Science Library |date=2016 |volume=440 |pages=1–60 |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-52859-4_1 |arxiv=1505.02172 |isbn=978-3-662-52857-0 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beloborodov |first1=A. M. |title=Super-Eddington Accretion Discs Around Kerr Black Holes |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=1998 |volume=297 |issue=3 |pages=739–746 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-8711.1998.01530.x |arxiv=astro-ph/9802129 |bibcode=1998MNRAS.297..739B |doi-access=free }}</ref> Accretion disks radiate across the entire [[electromagnetic spectrum]], depending on the disk's [[turbulence]] and [[magnetisation]] and the black hole's mass and angular momentum.<ref>{{multiref2|{{Cite journal |last1=Page |first1=Don N. |last2=Thorne |first2=Kip S. |title=Disk-Accretion Onto a Black Hole. Time-Averaged Structure of Accretion Disk |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=1974 |volume=191 |page=499 |doi=10.1086/152990 |bibcode=1974ApJ...191..499P }}|{{Cite journal |last1=Bisnovatyi-Kogan |first1=Gennady |title=Accretion into Black Hole, And Formation of Magnetically Arrested Accretion Disks |journal=Universe |date=2019 |volume=5 |issue=6 |page=146 |doi=10.3390/universe5060146 |arxiv=1905.13731 |bibcode=2019Univ....5..146B |doi-access=free }}|{{Cite journal |last1=Zakharov |first1=A. F. |last2=Repin |first2=S. V. |title=Model Radiation Spectrum for an Accretion Disk Near a Rotating Black Hole |journal=Astronomy Reports |date=2002 |volume=46 |issue=5 |pages=360–365 |doi=10.1134/1.1479423 |bibcode=2002ARep...46..360Z }}}}</ref>

Accretion disks can be defined as [[geometrical thickness|geometrically]] thin or geometrically thick.
